speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Finance this question. speechtext: I think this is a very important matter and I should like to ask the minister, in view of the fact that this is the fifth time in 12 months that the interest rate has been raised by the Bank of Canada, from 1-| per cent to 3i per cent, or almost a 125 per cent increase, whether the minister does not consider that such spectacular increases, coupled with other credit restrictions imposed upon the chartered banks now as directed by the Bank of Canada, may have a very dangerous and unsettling effect on the business and general economy of the country.

subtopic: BANK OF CANADA
subsubtopic: PURPOSE OF INCREASE IN INTEREST RATE
speechtext: The duty of the Bank of Canada is to regulate the interest rate, which is commonly known as the bank rate. That duty and responsibility is imposed upon the bank and not upon the government, and it has not been customary in the past for any Minister of Finance to comment on the actions of the bank in discharging its duty. As a matter of fact, however, without admitting some of the opinions or facts that have been stated in the question, I may say that there is a considerable body of opinion in the financial world today that unless action of this kind were taken there might be more serious results than if no action were taken.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue) moved
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 451, to amend the Canada-United States of America Tax Convention Act, 1943.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of these amendments in this Bill No. 451 is to clarify and to bring up to date the agreement for the avoidance of double taxation and the prevention of fiscal evasion relating to income tax. One item of importance in the convention reduces from 95 per cent to 51 per cent the percentage of share ownership entitling a United States parent company to a reduced rate of 5 per cent on dividends from its Canadian subsidiaries. The purpose of the amendment is to encourage United States parent corporations to give Canadian investors opportunities to purchase share ownership in their subsidiary companies in Canada.
Another item allows as a tax deduction charitable donations made by residents of one country to a charitable organization created in the other country. This supplementary convention will come into force as an integral part of the 1942 convention as modified by the 1950 convention with respect to taxation years beginning on and after the first day of January of the calendar year in which instruments of ratification of the convention are exchanged between the two governments.
Mr. Speaker, I do not feel that it is necessary to go into any long explanation of this bill. The bill in itself is very short, having but two subdivisions and there is attached to it a schedule which indicates that this convention has been signed on behalf of the government of Canada and the government of the United States. In the schedule the several articles which are modified are outlined. When we come to the schedule I shall be glad to attempt to give an explanation of the changes.

Mr. Speaker, as the minister has said, this is a very short bill. There are two clauses in the operative portion of it. To it is attached the new convention signed on August 8 with the United States of America.
The new convention itself contains a total of seven amendments to the 1942 Canada-United States tax convention, as amended by the convention of 1950. As to six of these 67509-4671
Canada-United. States Tax Convention Act amendments, I suppose it is fair to describe them as relating to matters of detail and administration raising no particular question of principle. But there is one amendment which involves what may properly be regarded as a matter of principle. It relates to the taxation of Canadian corporations which are subsidiaries of United States corporations. The change in the existing convention in this respect aims to encourage them to permit the sale to Canadian investors of the common stock of their Canadian subsidiaries. The principle of the bill, as so understood, is sound. The government's attempt to give effect to it is regrettably belated and hesitant. The purpose is sound, and we support the bill.
I have just a brief word to say on some features of this convention, Mr. Speaker, before concluding with some observations on this matter of investment in Canada through Canadian subsidiaries.
This is now the fifth measure which has come before this parliament in relation to tax conventions with the United States. The first convention of March 4, 1942, had for its purpose the avoidance of double taxation and the prevention of fiscal evasion in the case of income taxes. In 1944 came the second convention, along similar lines as applied to succession duties. In this respect, sir, there is an error in the bill, and I just point this out in passing now. The marginal note opposite the preamble refers to the 1944 act as though it had amended the 1942 convention. The reference to the 1944 act is to the one dealing with succession duties and it has nothing whatever to do with the matter now before us. Similarly, the marginal note is in error in referring only to the bill passed at the 1951, second session. The amendment to the convention of 1942 was made by the 1950 act and the 1951 bill which is referred to here was simply the Canadian acceptance of the United States rejection of paragraph 2 of article 7.
In my preliminary remarks, I said 1950.

Yes, 1950 is the important amendment to the 1942 convention. There was a further amendment in 1951 but the marginal note makes no reference to the 1950 statute and does refer to the 1944-45 statute, chapter 31, which has really no bearing on the tax convention relating to income taxes. It related purely to succession duties.
Our interest, of course, is in the treatment of Canadian subsidiaries taxwise under this convention. It is, however, reciprocal in its provisions and the amendments that are now
7354	HOUSE OF
Canada-United States Tax Convention Act before us for decision also cover the case of Canadian corporations which have subsidiaries in the United States.
It should be remembered that the ordinary rates of tax and all deductions at the source on dividends paid by Canadian corporations to shareholders resident abroad is 15 per cent, with some few exceptions. Article XI of the 1942 convention placed a limit of 5 per cent on the income tax which may be imposed by Canada on dividends paid by Canadian subsidiaries to United States parent corporations.
The 1942 convention contained a definition of subsidiaries and that definition, in effect, provided that a subsidiary was a corporation whose shares, apart from directors' qualifying shares, were wholly owned by an American corporation, with the exception that not more than a quarter of the gross dividends of the subsidiary should be derived from interest and dividends, other than interest and dividends received from its subsidiary corporations. This was the way the convention defined "subsidiary" until 1950, when the amendment of that year was approved by parliament by 1950 statutes, chapter 27, reducing the requirement from 100 per cent ownership of the stock of the Canadian subsidiary corporation to 95 per cent.
That is the provision which we are now asked to change further. The bill eliminates altogether the terms "parent" and "subsidiary". They disappear now entirely from the convention. "Subsidiary" becomes "payor corporation" and "parent" becomes "recipient corporation", that is to say, the recipient of the dividends from the payor corporation; and the percentage of required stock ownership in the Canadian subsidiary by the parent corporation is reduced from 95 per cent to 51 per cent. The provision continues, however, that it must be "at least" 51 per cent.
There is one further qualification. The 51 per cent does not now need to be owned entirely by one United States recipient corporation. Fifty-one per cent may be owned by four corporations, each with at least 10 per cent of voting stock of the payor corporation.
Now, sir, I wish to say just a word by way of putting the effect of this amendment in its true light. Let us see at once, then, that there is no change in the rate of taxation. The change that is brought about by this amending convention is in the percentage of stock in the Canadian subsidiary or payor corporation which must be held by the United States parent in order that the Canadian subsidiary may be subjected to an income tax rate not exceeding 5 per cent; whereas if the percentage of stock ownership by the


United States parent falls below 51 per cent, an income tax rate of 15 per cent is then applied on the dividends paid to it by the Canadian subsidiary corporation. Therefore, the United States corporation today which owns 100 per cent of the stock of a Canadian subsidiary is not affected. Likewise, a United States corporation which owns 95 per cent of the common or voting stock of a Canadian subsidiary corporation is not affected. In the case of United States corporations holding less than 51 per cent of stock of a Canadian subsidiary, there is no change. The Canadian subsidiary in the latter case still pays and deducts the 15 per cent rate on its dividends; but it is in the case of Canadian corporations whose voting stock between the 51 per cent mark and the 95 per cent mark is owned by United States parent corporations that the change is made. It is in this area that the change is effective, and corporations in this group will now obtain the benefit of the 5 per cent limit on income tax and also more combinations of United States corporations owning control of Canadian corporate subsidiaries may now qualify for the lower rate. There is, therefore, no advantage in the form of any tax reduction offered by this bill in the case of the wholly owned Canadian subsidiary. This bill simply means that in the case of the Canadian subsidiary, the United States corporation which controls ownership of its common or voting shares may dispose of shares in the Canadian corporation up to 49 per cent of the issued total without losing the benefit of the 5 per cent income tax rate. In other words, this is a negative form of encouragement to these Canadian corporations to sell some of their common stock to Canadian investors.
So far as foreign investment is concerned the bill affects only the United States, and only its corporate investors. There is today, it is estimated, about $11 billion of United States capital invested in Canada and that sum is constantly growing. We have had occasion in the past to pay tribute to the very useful and welcome part that United States capital has played in the development of Canadian resources. At the same time we Conservatives have taken advantage of all our opportunities to urge that there should be more and more Canadian investment participation in the ownership of corporations which are engaged in the development of the resources of this country.
That can be done in two ways. First it can be accomplished by increasing the proportion of Canadian total capital needs that is met out of domestic sources, and, in the second place, it can be done by adopting fair and

reasonable policies which will encourage nonCanadian owners of corporations to permit Canadian participation in the ownership of Canadian branch plants and subsidiary corporations.
This we have urged for some time. The kind of measure we have before us today was urged in the plainest terms by a great Canadian who on July 9, 1956, expressed it in these words as reported at page 5778 of Hansard:
Canadian tax laws should be changed to eliminate the tax penalty which a British or United States company must suffer when it allows Canadians to own a substantial minority interest in a wholly-owned Canadian subsidiary.
Those significant words were uttered, as I said, by a great Canadian, the Leader of the Opposition, and I am glad to see that the government has now seen fit to give heed to his wise words; for the time is certainly ripe to permit Canadians to participate more widely than has been the case heretofore in the purchase of the common stocks of Canadian subsidiary companies which are controlled by United States parent corporations.
This is no appeal based upon emotion. This is a proposal based upon sound logic and sound national objectives. On the boards of directors of these Canadian subsidiary corporations, in our view, there should be opportunities for wider Canadian participation. There should be more Canadians on the boards of directors of such corporations and more research should be done by such corporations in Canada.
This is a vast problem; for the extent of the ownership of corporations engaged in the development of Canadian resources is something that all hon. members would do well to ponder upon.
In the dominion bureau of statistics daily bulletin of July 6 this sentence appears. Speaking of the extent to which the ownership of stock of various lines of Canadian industry and resource development companies is in United States hands it says:
In manufacturing alone excluding petroleum refining the non-resident controlled portion in 1953 was some 47 per cent, and in petroleum 70 per cent, and in other mining 55 per cent. These percentages are much higher than formerly.
Therefore I say the time is ripe for measures of this kind. Mr. Muir, the president of the Royal Bank of Canada, sounded a note of warning and exhortation to Canadians on this subject last January when he said, as reported in the press:
Mr. Muir objected to the exclusion of Canadians from an ownership position in corporations doing business in Canada.
"Participation by Canadians in enterprises financed by outside (especially American) capital would be greatly encouraged were it not necessary
Canada-United States Tax Convention Act
in many cases to buy stock in the parent company in order indirectly to secure some voice in the operations of the Canadian subsidiary."
"In other words," Mr. Muir asserted, "Canadians should be allowed to buy stock directly in any Canadian corporation."
This measure should assist in that respect. It will at least give some encouragement in that direction. It is not going to produce wonders but it will give some encouragement. The same thought was stressed on May 24 by Mr. Crawford Gordon, president of Avro Canada Limited, speaking to the Canadian Club of New York, where he was reported as saying:
American companies setting up plants in Canada "would be wise to develop a higher degree of Canadian management" . . .
"U.S. capital is heartily welcome," he said. "Without it, much of our postwar development would not have occurred. But Canadians feel that too often that investment has taken the form of an American-managed branch operation."
He also urged American companies to permit a much wider stock participation in U.S. subsidiaries in Canada.
"This tendency to keep Canadian investors out is the subject of increasingly critical comment in our financial press. It is a factor, too, in the increasing concern being felt all over at the extent of total U.S. investment in Canada."
To the extent that this measure does indicate that parliament is aware of this problem, is concerned about it and wants to do something to point the way to United States corporations to enlarge the extent of Canadian participation in ownership of stock in their Canadian subsidiaries, it may be said now that this gives the United States corporations an opportunity, and in a sense puts a burden upon them, to busy themselves now and cut Canadians in on a larger share of the stock ownership and the consequent profits that are being made in this country. Mr. Ralph Blackmore, the financial editor of the Globe and Mail, in yesterday's issue said:
And now, as we say, we will see what happens. Readers know that we have been pounding this drum for a long time, our point being, now as when we started, that if a non-Canadian firm operates a successful subsidiary here, using Canadian manpower, materials, selling to Canadian customers and living under the protection of Canadian laws in a nation favourably disposed to private enterprise, that Canadians are entitled to a portion of the profits as share owners in those subsidiaries.
We of Her Majesty's loyal opposition share that point of view. We are glad to see that the policies that we have been advocating in this house and outside it have been in this respect adopted by the government. We say again that ours never was an appeal to mere emotion. Those who said so to your right, Mr. Speaker, and outside the house were completely mistaken in their assessment of the situation. Our policy never was based on mere emotion. It was based upon a sound

Canada-United, States Tax Convention Act view of what is the healthiest line for development of Canadian resources and Canadian participation in the ownership of those resources.
This measure is undoubtedly in response to a public demand for which we in the Conservative party have had the privilege of being the mouthpiece. Public thinking has been far ahead of governmental policy in this regard. We have deplored the delay. The measure could go further; we hope the government is not going to content itself simply with this as though it were a solution to the whole problem.
To the extent to which it will assist and give encouragement we approve it and support it, but we call upon the government to study the problem further with a view to taking other measures. There is one at least that is deserving of consideration. I realize this has to be a matter of negotiation with the United States authorities because it would have to be a matter of amendment of the convention, but thought ought to be given to setting up some form of graduation of the rates in relation to the extent of Canadian participation, so that within the permissible rates of taxation the rate would be reduced within those limits in accordance with certain specified proportions of Canadian ownership of the common or voting stock. That would give a more active and positive encouragement to a policy which, so far as this bill does give effect to it, is worthy of support.

There is one further thing I should like to mention, and this is really my reason for rising. It has to do with the question of the need for United States corporations expending in Canada a far greater amount for research than is the case today. The major portion of the research on the part of these great corporations in the United States operated in Canada is being done in the United States. That has the result of preventing many Canadian scientists, training chemists, physicists and the like from being employed within their own country and making their own contribution in Canada.
I know that a considerable number of scientifically trained Canadians have had to leave Canada to give the benefit of their talents to another country, although desirous of remaining in Canada.
I hope that this is but a step in the general direction and that everything will be done to the end that a fair proportion of the research expenditure by these corporations will be made in Canada so as thereby to allow Canadians, in the international economic race that the U.S.S.R. has now launched in all parts of the world, to provide that trained group of scientific personnel without which Canada cannot take its place in the international world.

I think it is unnecessary for me to say anything more and that those who have preceded me have set out the reasons why this legislation should be put through. I believe it is, as has been stated, a step in the right direction. We approve of it, and I think that is all we need to say.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue) moved
subtopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND WEST GERMANY FOR THE AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 452, to implement an agreement between Canada and the Federal Republic of Germany for the avoidance of double taxation with respect to income tax.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to give legal effect in Canada to the agreement which as the result of negotiations and subsequent exchanges has been reached between the government of Canada and the government of Germany for the avoidance of double taxation and the establishment of rules for reciprocal fiscal arrangements in the matter of income tax, which agreement

was signed at Ottawa on the fourth day of June, 1956. The provisions of this agreement are similar in their effect to those contained m the agreement which Canada has made with the United States, the United Kingdom, Sweden, New Zealand, France, Ireland and Denmark. It is designed to avoid double taxation and provides for exchange of information. By means of an exchange of reciprocal tax credits the country of residence gives credit for the tax in the country in which the actual income had its source. As in the other agreement taxation by a state on trade profits of an enterprise in the other state is limited to those attributable to the practical establishment of such enterprise in the first mentioned state. In addition, certain specific provisions are made regarding the profits from the operation of ships and aircraft and the exemption from tax on exchange of teachers and students.
I think that is all the explanation that I need to give at this time, Mr. Speaker. As I said, this is very similar to agreements that we have with other countries. As in the previous bill there is a schedule attached. If explanations are needed with reference to the changes in the schedule, I shall be very glad to give them.

subtopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND WEST GERMANY FOR THE AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Her Majesty's loyal opposition is always glad to support any measures that will give relief from taxation, and particularly, I suppose, relief from double taxation.
The bill follows the same form as those on earlier occasions with respect to other agreements. As the minister has said, Canada has similar tax agreements with the United States, the United Kingdom, Sweden, New Zealand, Denmark and France. The last of these agreements that was before us was the agreement with Ireland in February, 1955. The bill is identical in all respects with the bill to approve the tax convention with Ireland, although the convention itself is not at all identical with the Irish agreement. There will be some questions in relation to the differences. But as to the purpose of the bill, we are always in full sympathy with any measure to eliminate double taxation, to facilitate the exchange of information and to prevent tax evasions.

subtopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND WEST GERMANY FOR THE AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this group support this bill as a proper measure for arrangements between the two countries with respect to income taxation. However, I think this is an appropriate opportunity to bring certain things to the attention of the minister and the house. Last session, when I was trying to get away from the heat one Sunday afternoon,
I went out and sat down beside the bank

of the Ottawa river where the canal enters the river. While sitting there I had what I thought to be an old gentleman join me. I found out later that he was only something over 40 years of age, but that he had served six years in a German concentration camp. We got into quite a discussion. He gave me his life history. He told me of the fight for democracy in Germany and of things that had happened during his lifetime. During that conversation he mentioned to me that he had noticed that there was some indication that the Krupp interests were trying to establish subsidiary industries in Canada. I am not going to deal at length with what he had to say except to say this. He said, "I hope that you Canadians do everything you can to stop those people from entering your country. They have blighted Europe for a century."
The remarks I wish to make at the present time are, I know, supported by a large number of veterans in this country, a good many mothers and widows, and a large section of the Canadian public. From the women's paper Equality, which is the paper of the women's association of the German socialist party, I just want to read an extract as follows:
Shortly before the 1870-71 (Franco-German) war Krupp wrote to Napoleon urging him to order armaments from his plants. He sold armament secrets to the French before the first world war. He sold steel to the States at a cheaper rate than he did to his own country's navy. He sold the patent for a percussion fuse for high explosives to Vicker-Armstrong. After the war he demanded one shilling for every high explosive manufactured by that firm. High explosives which had killed thousands of German soldiers.
During the Chinese-Japanese war (1894) he sold arms to both sides and prevented the German government from taking part in united action to stop that war.
In 1914 the German government sent a protest note to the sultan because Krupps did not receive any armament contracts from him. They threatened to withdraw the German military mission. Another example of Krupps influence on German foreign policy.
In 1904 after England and France had settled their differences in Morocco, Krupp felt left out of things and persuaded the German government to land troops in Tangier.
Krupp together with other industrialists founded the "All German Association"	("Alldeutschen
Verband"). He was also active in the "German Naval Association" ("Deutschen Flotten Verein") and the "Army Association" ("Wehrverein") which called for the strengthening of German forces. The association's paper called for aggressive war and propagated the myth of German invincibility.
Krupp and other industrialists donated 500 million mark to the Freikorps. (That corps- was instrumental in bringing Hitler into power and helping him to remain there. E.C.) That same body donated 3 million mark after a secret meeting with Hitler in 1933. Krupps own words were that on behalf of the 25 industrialists present he would like to thank Hitler for the clear picture
Income Tax
he gave of his future plans. He also wrote to Hitler "that the changes on the political scene were in complete accord with his wishes and that of his directors".
On one or two occasions I have asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce if he knew whether the Krupps were attempting to establish an industry in Canada and he replied that he had no knowledge of that action being undertaken. However, I want to bring to the attention of the house some information contained in a copy of a letter written by Mr. A. Alex. Cattanach, director, companies division, to a lady who made inquiry with regard to this matter. It reads as follows:
Dear Miss McCaw:
I acknowledge receipt of your letter of July 8, 1958, in which you inquire concerning Ardelt Industries of Canada Limited.
A company of that name was incorporated by federal letters patent dated March 31, 1954.
The names and addresses of the directors were disclosed in the annual summary filed with this department as at March 31, 1956, as follows-
Dr. H. Herrmann, Essen, Germany.
Mr. Edward Volckmar, 200 St. Clair West, Toronto, Ontario.
J. Schroedar, Essen, Germany.
S. Ding, Wilhelmshaven, Germany.
A notification of the grant of the letters patent was published in the issue of the Canada Gazette dated April 17, 1954.
The application for incorporation was supported ",y- " consent thereto executed by Ardeltwerke G.M.B.H. of Welhelmshaven.
Yours very truly,
A. Alex. Cattanach,
Director, Companies Division.
in that connection I should like to point out to the house and to the minister that the name of J. Schroedar, Essen, Germany, should bring to their attention the fact that that name is very closely associated with the Krupps industry over there. I have here some photostatic copies of an interview with this gentleman in which he does some whining about the treatment the Krupps industry received at the hands of the allies after the war. While the minister has not any knowledge of this, and I am quite sure he has not, we find a press dispatch from the Cornwall Standard-Freeholder of June 2, 1956, after this matter was raised in the house. It says: Dr. Hans Weddingen, commercial attache of the German embassy here, has lent support to reports a Canadian subsidiary of the giant Krupps steel works of Essen, Germany, plans a major steel industry on the shores of the St. Lawrence river near Cornwall.
Then, it quotes the commercial attache:
"I know they (Krupps) have something in mind for Canada,"-
I hope it is not what they had in mind for other countries.
-he said Friday. "Their first intention was to do something in Labrador but they changed their mind."

Income Tax
He said he believes there will be confirmation within a year of reports that the Krupps Canadian firm of Krupps-Ardelt plans to build a giant steel plant in the Cornwall area.
Agents in Cornwall Thursday said options have been taken on five large farms in the area.
Krupps of Essen Friday denied the reports a steel plant was planned on the St. Lawrence.
But Dr. Weddingen said "this is typical of German industry".
"First there is a story, then a denial, then silence for a while and they start building a plant."
I think this is a firm which we should indicate is not welcome in Canada. We can get investment capital from other industries outside of this country if we require it. This firm has blighted the history of Europe for 100 years. I am afraid if they are allowed in this country they will continue the same machinations they continued in Europe during that time and right up to the present time. They have plants in Spain. The very publicity advisers to Nasser in Egypt were formerly associated with this firm. They are expanding into Indonesia and looking for opportunities in Asia. They are looking for opportunities and think Canada is a ripe plum to pick.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I could give voluminous evidence as to the history of this firm but I am not going to do that. I am merely going to quote from the Montreal Star of February 10, 1946. This article was written by Mr. DeWitt Mackenzie. It reads:
This house of Krupp was created from the profits of war piled up through the generations, and in this sense it was built on the bodies of men who died in battle that Krupps might prosper.
History pins the responsibility for much of German aggression during the past century on Krupp's and it will be history which will tell us how many conflicts this firm fed among Germany's neighbours.
It was Alfred Krupp, founder of the firm, who provided the sinews of war for Germany's onslaught against France in 1870. It was Krupp's which carried Kaiser Wilhelm on its back to near victory over the Allies in the First Great War. And it was Krupp's that was one of the main contributors-perhaps the main one-to Hitler's all but successful attempt to conquer Europe. . . .
One could write a book about the villa Hugel, but the purpose of this article is to draw attention to an aspect of German aggression which we don't see emphasized fully enough. This is that militarism has been supported by and encouraged by the titan armament firm of Krupp, which has been the motor of the war machine.
All members of this house welcome any democrat who wishes to come to this country to live here and help it develop. We have a good many democratic Germans who have come in recent years. I have had conversations with many of them and I know what they have suffered. I know their attitude towards a firm such as Krupps, and its effect on German and European history for the last 100 years. We should welcome all these people but in my opinion, Mr. Speaker,

fully realizing the difficulties as between the federal and provincial jurisdiction, I urge this government to indicate that this firm is unwelcome in Canada. To permit this company, with a century of blood-stained hands, to come into this country and assist us to develop is morally wrong, thoroughly unsound, and is putting blinkers on ourselves with respect to the history of its past.

and the Canadian National Railways, each trying to pass the buck with hon. members from Newfoundland adding something to it by way of general background, and altogether we get a pot-pourri which the minister with his vivid imagination and his experience in the opposition will realize it is very difficult for a poor person sitting over here not having access to all the government reports to fully understand.
I am endeavouring to get this down to a simple compass this morning and I do not want to indulge in any pyrotechnics or anything of the kind. What I am trying to find out is just where this matter now stands.
The Minister of Public Works is reported in the press as having said that the breakwater had been completed and the sum of $186,000 is the figure used in the press. I do not know whether or not that is correct. The report also says that a 600 foot breakwater had been put in at Port aux Basques harbour and apparently the Minister of Public Works intimated that the next step was for the C.N.R. to have the William Carson make a test run or two into the terminal to see whether it could be accommodated in the harbour with the new installation.
I do not want to offend the delicate feelings of the minister in this matter, as I say, and so I shall say that in addition to the breakwater which was to be built-the minister can call it what he will-the national research council were asked to erect a model of Port aux Basques harbour in which experiments could be conducted. We have now reached a situation where the Minister of Public Works says that we have reconstructed it or constructed it-
That is better.
Yes, I will use the term "constructed", if you like.
Well, use the accurate one.

All right, I will use the accurate term. God constructed the first breakwater and then someone removed it and the Minister of Public Works has constructed a new one and now the Minister of Public Works says to the C.N.R., "Why don't you use the harbour for a test run?" According to the press the C.N.R. says, "No, we do not want to use the harbour". I am not attempting to quote the press report but according to it the Department of Transport and the C.N.R. have suggested to the Department of Public Works that the trial runs for the William Carson be postponed and that the Department of Public Works should conduct further tests on the $70,000 national research council hydraulic model. One would almost infer, Mr. Chairman, that the C.N.R. and

Supply-Transport
the Department of Transport were not certain that the expenditures on the harbour were completed and that they required further tests to be made on the harbour.
In any event there is apparently some difference of opinion between the two departments with respect to this matter. The Minister of Transport may be justified in this and I am not criticizing him for it but it almost appears as if he or his departmental officials felt that the situation at the Port aux Basques harbour is such that they do not want to operate the ferry there until the tests are carried out on the model. According to the statement which was issued some time ago, this could not be done until September. It is certainly a matter of importance as to when this can be done and I would like to have the minister clarify the situation if he would.
I am always amused when I hear the hon. member talk about Port aux Basques and the William Carson-
If you were impressed I would be much more comforted.

-particularly as he draws liberally on his imagination in order to add humour to what he has to say. If we could get back to the facts of the matter, perhaps it would be easier for the committee to understand exactly what the situation is at Port aux Basques. Perhaps I should say this to the hon. gentleman who has just spoken. If he had not made the several humorous speeches on the subject of the William Carson that he made during the last session and on every conceivable occasion, I think there would have been much less confusion in the minds of the public as to what is the real situation. As someone who has experienced political life in opposition, I think that the hon. gentleman should feel a certain satisfaction in having added this element of confusion to the situation.
I cannot compete with the minister in that respect.
There was plenty of confusion before he started.
You dispel it, if you will.

After these preliminaries, I shall try to do exactly that. I shall not promise that the hon. member will understand but I shall give him an opportunity at least of knowing the facts. The first thing I should like to say is about the $413,000 which is covered by this vote. This is not in connection with the dredging but it is, as I

understand it, the cleaning up of the expenditures in connection with the construction of the new dock and terminal facilities at Port aux Basques.
Hon. members will recall that we discussed the subject of Port aux Basques approximately towards the end of the last session of parliament and at that time, I think, I told the committee that we were going to retain the services of an expert in order to advise us as to the situation in Port aux Basques harbour. I should like first of all to correct an impression, which somehow or other has got around, that the work that was done in Port aux Basques was such that there was not enough water for the Carson to go in. That has not been the case, and at no time has that been the problem.
I have a very delightful cartoon that appeared in the Gazette of my trying to get the William Carson down a chimney, and the Carson obviously was much too big for the chimney. All I can say is that the cartoonist, who has an excellent reputation as an artist, must have been inspired by the hon. gentleman who has just spoken on this item, because if he had been inspired by the facts he would not have drawn the cartoon at all.
After the last session ended, I asked the high commissioner in London if he would be good enough to ascertain what experts in matters of harbour engineering might be available at short notice to visit Port aux Basques and to examine the situation from beginning to end. I want to say right away that I did not seek somebody in England because there was no one available in Canada, but I am sure hon. members will agree that there was no one available in Canada who had no association either with the government or with the Canadian National Railways. I felt that it was desirable to have someone who had no attachments of any kind and whose impartiality and independence could not reasonably be challenged.
The expert who was appointed, after we had made these inquiries, was Mr. R. D. Gwyther, who is one of the senior partners of the firm known as Coode and Partners. It was interesting to learn that one of the predecessor members of this firm had had a connection with Port aux Basques many years before; not that that was material to the case, but it was merely a matter of interest. When I met Mr. Gwyther, about a year ago, the first thing I told him was that I wanted to get from him a completely independent report and that I was not asking him to justify what had been done. I wanted to know what were the facts and whether a mistake had been made.
Hon. members perhaps should realize that the obligation to establish a service between

North Sydney and Port aux Basques results from the terms of union with Newfoundland. The obligation was that of providing services which would accommodate passengers, automobiles and cars. I am not talking about these two places except so far as the distance between them is concerned. That obligation necessitated the building of a ship which would be speedy and which would load and unload rapidly so that the round trip between North Sydney and Port aux Basques could be covered within the least possible time so as to make the operation as economic as possible. That accounts for the dimensions of the Carson and the necessity for having a vessel strengthened for ice and having high power, and, because of the desirability of rapid loading and unloading, the rather complex arrangement of the facilities at the terminals both at North Sydney and at Port aux Basques. That very factor of special facilities prevents the Carson from being used just anywhere at any time.
If I might return to my conversation with Mr. Gwyther, I asked him to make an exhaustive study of the matter and to give me a completely impartial report. One of the first things that Mr. Gwyther considered was whether or not the dredging that was done between Pikes and Vardys islands had been harmful to the situation. I was jesting a moment ago when I spoke of the hon. member, but an impression has been created that the dredging that was done between these two islands ruined the harbour. I believe that the hon. member, when speaking on the estimates of the Department of Public Works, quoted some newspaper article, though how the word "ruined" ever got into the newspaper article I find it difficult to say. No one has used that word authoritatively, and it will certainly not be found in the Gwyther report. The rather liberal interpretation put on the Gwyther report certainly does not find any justification in the actual words he used. I should like to read from the Gwyther report his comment with regard to the channel between these two islands. He says, in paragraph 9:
The channel which existed between Vardys island and Pikes island has been enlarged to give a minimum depth of 23 feet at low water for a width of 350 feet. This dredging increased the cross sectional area of the original channel by only 17 to 20 per cent and we cannot believe that this caused any appreciable increase in the ranging at the new wharves.
I did not dictate that paragraph to Mr. Gwyther, and I think that is a fair comment on the situation that exists in Port aux Basques harbour. The whole difficulty that we have had to meet is the fact that the facilities as they now exist in Port aux Basques harbour are such that there is not the quiet
Supply-Transport
water that should be expected for a ship of this dimension which is going to be moored at the terminal We asked Mr. Gwyther what work ought to be undertaken in order to provide a quiet harbour for the William Carson, and I might just read another paragraph from the report, paragraph 12, which reads as follows:
12. Suggestions have been made for Improving these conditions and are as follows:
(i)	to close the channel between Vardys and Pikes island and to widen the approach channel on the west side of Vardys island and between the middle and west Baldwin rocks;
(ii)	to construct breakwaters at the Baldwin rocks closing the channel between the middle and west Baldwin and enlarge the channel eastward of the east Baldwin;
(iii)	to construct a short breakwater running northeast from Vardys island leaving the new channel clear and widening the existing channel between Vardys island and Pancake rock and at the Baldwins.
I am not going to read the whole report, which is somewhat lengthy, but the point I should like to emphasize is that these suggestions were considered by Mr. Gwyther, and his recommendation will be found in paragraph 14 which I shall read:
14. We strongly recommend that a model should be made of the harbour and the effect produced by the construction of breakwaters tested on the model. This need not delay the start of work on the landward breakwater or on the improvement of the channel between Vardys island and Pancake rock.
The breakwater which has been constructed does not replace anything that existed before. It is something that is entirely new, and that was the reason why I objected to the rather liberal interpretation which the hon. gentleman placed on the facts of the matter just a few moments ago. This is a new breakwater. Mr. Gwyther recommended that we should build a model and that we should at the same time build this breakwater which he considers would be essential.
As hon. members know, the Department of Public Works has built the model and model tests have been continuing and are still continuing. The hon. gentleman seemed to imply from some clippings that have been read from the newspapers that the national research council has reached some conclusions. I hope I am not wrong in that inference I took from what the hon. gentleman said, but that is not in conformity with the facts. No report has been made by the national research council as to the result of its studies. However, I should like to tell hon. members of the committee that there may have been formed in the minds of some of those who are conducting the studies some preliminary ideas that the studies and tests so far have developed. But so far as my department is concerned, and I consider we are very vitally interested

Supply-Transport
in the matter, we have no report whatever as to the conclusions to be reached from the model studies that have been undertaken up to the present.
I made some inquiries this week to find out what was the state of affairs so that it would be possible for us to know what progress was being made, and I was told that it was hoped that the report would be available within a matter of two or three weeks. I think the hon. gentleman will probably realize that what Mr. Gwyther had in mind in recommending the construction of the model was to tell from the model where other protective works should be placed if other protective works were necesary after the construction of the breakwater which has since been built and completed.
We have not yet got the results of these studies and consequently we are not in a position to say today-I regret it very much -just what further works, if any, require to be done in the harbour so as to make it entirely usable by the William Carson. I understand there has been comment in the press, or perhaps I should call it speculation, as to trial runs for the William Carson. I have discussed this subject with the Department of Public Works and with the Canadian National Railways, and I was under the impression a few days ago that arrangements had been concluded by the Canadian National Railways and public works to make some trial runs. But this week I took the trouble to verify the exact situation and when I found that definite arrangements had not been made I asked that a meeting be convened of all of the parties interested, national research council, public works, Canadian National Railways and officials of my department, in order that the matter should be examined fully so that we could see whether it was desirable to have trial runs of the Carson into Port aux Basques. That will be the subject of discussion at a meeting to be held next week.
But the point I should like to emphasize particularly, because I do not think it is desirable that wrong impressions should arise from carrying out trial runs, is that a trial run must for all practical purposes be carried out with a ship that is carrying neither freight, automobiles nor passengers. It is not possible to organize it for passengers for the simple reason that it would be an entirely new service and there is no reason why passengers should participate in it. Naturally what we have in mind is the commencement of the service just as soon as we can be certain that the harbour will be a safe, quiet harbour for the Carson while she is in service there. Consequently, if it is decided that the Carson will make trial runs as part of the
[Mr. Marler.l
studies which are in process by the national research council no one should expect that she will be used for the carrying of passengers, freight or automobiles. It is a technical test, and I take it that those who participate in it will be the technical officials of the four bodies interested that I mentioned a moment ago.
I have no hesitation in confessing that I had really hoped after I had seen Mr. Gwyther in August of last year and had read his report, received some time around the middle of August, that the model studies would have been completed long before this and we would have had a conclusive report as to what ought to be done in order to settle the matter fully and finally.
Are they being done here in Ottawa?

Yes, they are being done in Ottawa. I have not seen them personally. Unfortunately time seems to be so much at a premium that I have not been able to get out to see them. I do not suggest that my going out there would make any difference to the studies but I had hoped to see them and I had hoped that they would have led to a conclusive report before this. However, my hopes have been disappointed. But I do hope it will not be long before we have a definite recommendation as to what works must be done.
I do not blame the opposition for the fact that the impression has been created by them that the government has made a mistake in this matter. I am quite sure if I had been a member of the opposition I would have done my utmost to create that impression.
We do not have to create it.

I will leave the hon. gentleman with his opinion, but perhaps people who will take an impartial, objective view of the facts might not agree. I do not blame the opposition for endeavouring to create the impression that there has been a grave mistake, but perhaps the grave mistake was in agreeing that Port aux Basques should be the northern terminal of this route. But, Mr. Chairman, that is a fact; that is part of the terms of union. The terms of union provide that the service shall be between Port aux Basques and North Sydney, not between North Sydney and some other place in Newfoundland. It is my personal conviction that, having chosen Port aux Basques, we were, perhaps unconsciously at that time but fatally committed to provide that kind of service and to do so on the most economic terms possible, committed to doing the physical works in the harbour which will cost us a great deal.
May I ask a question? Was there ever any attempt made by the dominion government to negotiate with Newfoundland for a change to some other port?
Mr. Chairman, I am handicapped by the fact that I was not a party to the negotiations in 1949. I do not know what considerations entered into the discussions at that time.
Perhaps the minister can find that out at the noon adjournment.

I feel perfectly sure that it was chosen because of the factor of distance and because of the factor of the railway; in other words, that there were certain obvious reasons why Port aux Basques had to be chosen. My understanding of the matter is that it really was not possible to consider establishing the service to another point. When one looks at the map, I think one cannot help concluding that the service had to be provided between those two points. Having reached that conclusion, the question then arose as to the kind of ship. If you provide a smaller vessel, then you cannot accommodate passengers, freight and automobiles as the terms of union call for, in the same volume, let us say, as is to be provided in the William Carson.

Was there any agreement
between Canada and Newfoundland with regard to the type and size of ship?

No; there was not. But I suggest to the hon. gentleman that the undertaking to carry freight, automobiles and passengers, coupled with the fact that you had to provide a rapid turn-around in order to accomplish the operation in 24 hours, imposed certain conditions that had to be met, certain physical conditions that could not be met in any other way than those provided by the William Carson itself.
The minister is not suggesting that Newfoundland is in any way responsible for the fact that the ship was built but could not use the harbour? He is not doing that, is he?

No, I am not suggesting any such thing as that at all. I am merely suggesting that, having laid down these specifications, the economics dictated that you should have a fairly large vessel, powerful, able to operate during the winter months, able to carry passengers, freight and automobiles, and to meet the necessity of rapid loading and unloading. I suggest that when you read these specifications and when you say the service must be between Sydney and Port aux Basques, then you are fatally led to the situation which now exists. Had we
Supply-Transport
been so foresighted and so gifted as to have complete information as to Port Aux Basques, it is quite possible that we would have said at the time of union, "We will have to spend a great deal of money on the harbour in order to provide for the facilities which are called for under the terms of union." I am sorry but I do not know how much the breakwater that has been constructed has cost. I think perhaps the matter was dealt with on the estimates of the Department of Public Works, as it is an expenditure of that department. I do not know what further works will have to be built. All I can say is that we will know when the model studies are completed. I hope they will show us that the work that remains to be done is not of major dimensions.
Mr. Chairman, I am sorry I am taking so long on this item but I want to repeat that I think it is perfectly clear to an impartial person that the relatively small amount of dredging that was done in the channel between Pikes island and Vardys island has had no substantial effect on the harbour itself.

I do not think the minister needs to apologize for the time he has spent on this item. I realize that the committee is working under pressure and no one wants to delay it, I least of all. I do not propose to enlarge on the matter at any undue length and I am not going to indulge to any imaginative or pyrotechnic speech as the minister almost invited me to do. I refrain from doing that. But this is a matter of tremendous importance to all eastern Canada, as well as to the province of Nova Scotia. The confederation pact with Newfoundland has been in abeyance and is now, one might say, dishonoured because we are not fulfilling our obligations there at all in so far as transportation is concerned back and forth between Newfoundland and eastern Canada, and, I presume, all of Canada, having regard to anyone who ships to Newfoundland. The situation is just one horrible mess. That is the only way in which it can be described.
The minister speaks about the opposition and rather pays it the compliment of having created-and I emphasize the word "created" -an impression that there was something wrong in connection with this matter. We certainly have not created it, Mr. Chairman. There is not a newspaper you can read in eastern Canada or a newspaper in Newfoundland that has not stressed that fact. In my opinion we have been, as usual, very conservative in our statements and in our approach to this matter. If there has been any touch of humour at all, it is only because we felt so sympathetic with the minister who was loaded down with such a tragic error that we

Sup p ly-Transport
felt that if we really dealt with the thing too seriously he might feel that he should be called upon to resign or something of that kind. So perhaps when mentioning it I will introduce a little bit of humour in order to lighten the load which otherwise he would carry.
Do that.
I have here an editorial-I am not going to read it-from the Cape Breton Post of August 2 dealing with this matter. It says that everything is a fog with respect to the William Carson.
It is what?

It reads:
Everything having to do with the operation of the splendid new ferry, William Carson, between North Sydney and Newfoundland, continues to be wrapped in mystery, as if an impenetrable fog descended every time the circumstances arise for lucid explanation.
Then it goes on to say this:
It has ceased to be funny, this is to say if anyone ever found it amusing.
Articles have appeared in the Halifax Herald, in the Newfoundland papers and all the rest. I am not going to accept for one second the suggestion that the opposition are responsible for having enlarged on this matter in any way. There are a few facts about this matter which I want to get clear, and we shall not have time to do it before one o'clock. After all, if there is a touch of humour in the matter, it is in the minister's statement this morning. I wish I had Hansard before me. He, of course, always has a delicate touch. The minister spoke almost sadly about the fact-I have forgotten some of the words-that the facilities at Port aux Basques did not lend themselves to, shall we say, a smooth harbour. I think that was the effect of what he said. He spoke as if this came as a great surprise and a great shock. That, of course, is as humorous as anything could be. Apparently, they never heard of John Sebastian Cabot who discovered Newfoundland and who reported that Port aux Basques was a pretty tricky harbour. Of course there was another John Sebastian Cabot Pickersgill who made a discovery. I am not sure whether he discovered Newfoundland or whether Newfoundland discovered him. But certainly he knew that Port aux Basques was far from being a smooth harbour.
The minister says we are under an obligation to carry cars, to carry passengers and to carry freight. They certainly are not carrying out the obligation, are they? That ship cannot do it under the existing situation. If errors were made in accepting Port

aux Basques-if you were bound to accept it, and I think there is some merit in that suggestion; there was a railway connection there-instead of having that palatial liner which was too big for the harbour, I think that serious consideration should have been given to having two small boats as recommended by the Newfoundland captains, seamen, fishermen and press.
I can tell the hon. gentleman that I have heard often about that so-called recommendation but nobody seems to have found it in my department or in the Canadian National Railways.
That is why the Cape Breton Post says there is such a fog.
Let us stick to the facts.

I do not want to be unkind, but the Cape Breton Post says that the Minister of Transport apparently has not even heard from his colleague the Minister of Public Works about the fact that he wants the boat to make a trial run or runs into the harbour.
That is pure conjecture and without foundation.

It may be conjecture but at least that is not disseminated by the opposition. Those are statements that have been made. What we want to do this afternoon and in perhaps three or four minutes after this committee reconvenes is to have the minister tell us what is going to be done and when, and also what it has cost us so far. He says that he is still waiting, as I understand it, and that he feels that there should be further experiments carried out or tests with respect to the working model of the harbour.
I wish the hon. gentleman would stick to what I said. It would make it much easier for me.
Is that not what the minister said?
No. I told the hon. gentleman that we were waiting until the present studies are completed by the national research council.
That is what I said.

It is not a question of further studies. Surely the hon. gentleman understands that we are still talking about studies that were initiated to determine what works ought to be done in order to make Port aux Basques a quiet harbour.

I am not going to engage in a dialectical discussion with the minister

with regard to the word "further". I accept his word that they are waiting to learn the results of the study. I realize that you have only one study and that there are no further studies. The only comment I have to make is that they built the harbour for a certain type of operation and then they decided to build a working model and to make studies. Now the studies are not over. After lunch I should like it if the minister would please fell us when they can operate that service and if he can give any intelligent-I do not mean "intelligent" unkindly-any relatively accurate estimate of what can be done.

I do not want to spoil the hon. gentleman's lunch but I cannot add anything to what I have already said. He knows, just as I do, the danger of making promises as to dates and holding out expectations that might prove to be wholly unjustified. I may be spoiling his lunch, but I can add nothing this afternoon to what I have already said.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the minister can answer a few questions with respect to this item of $413,000 which is for, as I said earlier, the construction of new dock and terminal facilities at Port aux Basques, Newfoundland, during this coming year? Can the minister tell us what has been spent to date on the new dock and terminal facilities in so far as it comes within his department, or of which he has knowledge, and also what is proposed to be done with the $413,000 this year?

Well, Mr. Chairman, I am not in a position to give the absolutely final detail but I would like to tell the hon. gentleman that the expenditure to March 31, 1955, was $5,067,223. The estimated expenditure for 1955-56 is $369,140; the estimated requirement for 1956-57 is $413,000; the estimated requirement for 1957-58 is $470,000, making a total of $6,319,363. To that must be added a further amount payable by Canadian National Railways of $488,000, making an estimated total cost, which includes the provision of modern freight handling equipment of $6,807,363.

Does that include the cost of the containers of which we have spoken before?
Supply-Transport

No, I do not think it does, Mr. Chairman. My deputy minister points out that half of the total cost of the containers is included in the total estimated cost that I have just given, and the other half of the cost of the containers is included in the costs in the Sydney area.
Does that include all expenditures made by the Department of Public Works as well?
No, these are transport or C.N.R.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

I have one other question before the item does carry. As I understand it, from what the minister said this morning, there will be an interdepartmental meeting next week between his department, public works and I think he said the Canadian National Railways and national research, and at that meeting it would be determined if and when a trial run or runs would be instituted by the Carson into Port aux Basques harbour. Is that correct?

I think I should make a purely verbal correction in what the hon. gentleman has just said. I am not asking the officials to make a decision. I ask them to make a recommendation but I shall take the responsibility.
Surely. No decision will be taken till next week, and no decision has been taken at the moment.

No. I would like to emphasize, because of the news that has appeared in the press, that at no time has any decision been taken. Consequently, there has been no postponement. The date has not been fixed. I hope-if that seems the intelligent thing to do-we shall come to some decision next week.
Is this a fair question? Is the minister in a position to give any intimation as to when he would expect the Carson would start regular service to Port aux Basques?
I think the question is a perfectly fair one, but I am unable to give a fair answer.

Item agreed to.

To provide for the payment during the fiscal year 1956-57 to the Canadian National Railway Company (hereinafter called the national company) upon applications approved by the Minister of Transport made from time to time by the national company to the Minister of Finance and to be applied by the national company in the payment of the deficit (certified by the auditors of the national company) in the operation of ferry and terminal services between North Sydney. Nova Scotia and

Port aux Basques, Newfoundland, and on a temporary basis between North Sydney, Nova Scotia and Argentia, Newfoundland and between North Sydney, Nova Scotia and other Newfoundland ports, arising in the calendar year 1956, $3,4S6,250.

This is the deficit item for the operation of the William Carson for the year. This is for the calendar year 1956, or arising in the calendar year 1956. I believe there is an item in the supplementary estimates of $1,100,000, which would make in all $4,596,250. The detail speaks of the calendar year 1956, but the item says, "fiscal year 1956-57". Can that be clarified?

I do not want the two items to be added together because that will give a misleading impression. First of all, I would like to emphasize that this item of $3,496,250, covers the deficit of all of the ferry operations, all of the Newfoundland railway and steamship services, North Sydney, Port aux Basques, Argentia and other Newfoundland ports, and not just the William Carson, and the figures are for the calendar year 1956. If the hon. member would like to have a breakdown, they represent $2,925,000, being the estimated deficit for 1956 on the service between North Sydney and Port aux Basques. This deficit excludes the Carson because she is not in that service at the moment; approximately $500,000 for the service in which the Carson is running for purposes of freight between North Sydney and Argentia, and $71,250 for services between North Sydney and other Newfoundland ports. Now, there are some other figures covered in the supplementaries. Perhaps we can deal with them when the supplementaries are called, but they are not for the same purpose.
What is included in the deficit? Is that something of an operating item or does it include interest and sinking fund?
This is a straight operating deficit and it does not include interest.
Can the minister tell us what was the total capital cost of the Carson so that we can-
I have not the figure immediately at hand, but it is somewhat slightly in excess of $11 million.
Perhaps the minister can get the total.
I will have a look for it and I will give it.

The minister said it does include the deficit on the existing service

between North Sydney and Port aux Basques as well as the operating deficit on the Carson itself.

I have just given those figures: on the North Sydney and Port aux Basques run, $2,925,000; between North Sydney and Argentia-that is the Carson-$500,000 and the other ports, $71,250. The exact cost of the Carson is $11,243,000.
That deficit on the service between North Sydney and Port aux Basques is exclusive of any deficit on the Carson at all; it is on the other small ships that operate?
Yes.
Can the minister give the figure for the deficits on the earlier years of the operation of the Carson?
There were no earlier years for the operation of the Carson.
This vote is for 1956?
Yes.
What about 1955?

The operations of the
Carson for 1955 are covered by the supplementary vote, and perhaps we can deal with it when we get to that item.

Item agreed to.
461.	Construction or acquisition of auto-ferry vessels and equipment as listed in the details of the estimates, provided that treasury board may increase or decrease the amount within the vote to be expended upon individual listed projects, $1,914,000.
What is proposed in this item? Can the minister give us a breakdown?
