The item includes also $250,000 of the expenditures on the Carson; $500,000 for the Bluenose; and $44,000 for construction or acquisition of equipment.
That is additional expenditure made on the Carson?
No; these are included in the total I gave the hon. gentleman a moment ago.

Item agreed to.
462.	Yarmouth, Nova Scotia-Bar Harbor, Maine, U.S.A., ferry service-deficit, 1956, $230,000.

This item, Mr. Chairman, covers the operating deficit of the motor vessel Bluenose operating between Bar

Harbor and Yarmouth. Again 1 would ask the
minister if that simply covers the operating amount or if it includes any charge for depreciation or interest on the Bluenose. I also wonder if the minister could now give us the total cost of the Bluenose, the amount that was paid toward that cost by the province of Nova Scotia, and then after I receive that information there is one other comment I want to make in respect to it.

The estimated deficit of $230,000 is very largely an operating deficit. I would like to mention that in the operating expenses the following items are included which are perhaps not wholly an operating expense in the ordinary sense of the word. There is a fee to the Canadian National Railways of $35,000, interest on working capital $7,000 and $61,000 for the amortization of loans, making a total of $103,000 that strictly speaking might be considered not to be an operating expense.
What loans?
These are in connection with the facilities at Bar Harbor and at Yarmouth.
It is money borrowed for the construction of those facilities?
Yes.

I do not think anyone can criticize the size of the deficit for the first year in which that was in operation.
I would like to make one or two suggestions to the minister. He has just told us that the Canadian National is getting an operating fee in connection with this boat. I have heard from some people-some of whom are in the range of our voices now who propose to travel on that boat-about what anpears to be a rather anomalous situation.
If the minister proposed to go across on the Bluenose as a passenger I understand that he could make a reservation in Ottawa for a certain day and embark his car and go across but he cannot buy his ticket here for some reason or other. I think this is a minor thing that should be rectified because it causes a lot of irritation.
I know civil servants here in Ottawa who have gone across there within the last few weeks. They could not buy a ticket at the C.N.R. office in Ottawa. When they arrived at Bar Harbor they had to buy their ticket there and pay excise tax to the state of Maine on their ticket to travel on a Canadian ship which was built by Canadian money. I think that is just carelessness somewhere possibly on the part of Canadian National administration.
Supply-Transport
I will be perfectly frank and say that I took this up with the passenger department in Ottawa because certainly they have always given me the greatest co-operation and I did not wish to say anything by way of criticizing them.
Recently I had occasion to go to California. I bought a ticket here from the Canadian Pacific to go to San Francisco and to return to Ottawa. They gave me what they call a prepaid voucher and thereby I saved a few dollars in excise tax which I would have had to pay to the state of California.
Tax evasion.

If that can be done in the state of California I think it could also be done in the state of Maine. As I have said it has caused some irritation. I think the excise tax is 15 per cent. I do not see any reason in the world why people going from Canada and travelling into the United States are compelled to buy a ticket in Bar Harbor and pay excise tax to the state of Maine. I think this is one matter that should be rectified before another year elapses.
Another matter I would like to mention is something which I spoke to the minister about a year ago. The minister, as I recall it, indicated that this was being done on a trial basis and I want to remind him again of the present system whereby the boat ties up in Bar Harbor, goes over to Yarmouth and then back to Bar Harbor. I think the minister told us at one time they were trying this-I am not trying to quote or paraphrase him in any way-but I think the effect of his statement was that we were going to try it and that it was likely or possible that we would change it, depending on the experience. I hope the experience has been such that the department is considering changing the present system.
There are several reasons that could be advanced which make a change desirable. One reason is that the crew is practically all Canadian and is made up of Nova Scotians and they are compelled to live in Bar Harbor because they tie up there every night. Another matter is that Canadian and United States tourists have to stay in Maine at Bar Harbor overnight. This is good for the hotel keepers and hostels at Bar Harbor. More than one United States tourist in my own town tell me that when they started on two weeks' vacation they would have preferred to spend the first night of that vacation in what they called "a foreign country", in other words Canada; but they have to go to Bar Harbor, stay there overnight, get up at 4.30 in the morning and catch the boat.

Supp ly-Transport
There are several other reasons that could be advanced. This present system is detrimental to the hotel business in the western part of Nova Scotia. Perhaps there is some advantage in it to my triends in the eastern part of the province who can get in their cars and catch the boat at 2.30 in the afternoon, but the present system results in a fairly substantial loss to the people of western Nova Scotia. Some Americans have told me that when they started their vacation they would have preferred to spend the first night in Canada, a foreign country, rather than in Maine. I think this is something the minister could again review and see if, having tried it on the present basis, a change could be made in order to learn whether a new system would be just as effective.
The third suggestion I mentioned a year ago is this. There has been a great deal of criticism concerning the rates which are imposed on truck transport on the boat. I realize that transport rates are fixed by various yardsticks, one of which is what the traffic will bear. Certainly in the summer time when the tourist season is on the traffic will meet the rates which are now being imposed because there are reservations every day and the boat could probably carry many more cars than it has facilities to carry; but some time around the middle of September the volume of traffic is going to fall off rapidly and I suspect the boat will not have such a heavy loading. At the same time there is going to be an increase in the trucks going from Nova Scotia to New England, particularly this year, because of an abnormal situation which has developed whereby the apple crop in many parts of the United States has been hurt by frost. There is every indication that barring hurricanes there is going to be a substantial movement of apples and other farm products as well from Nova Scotia into the markets of New England, and this presents an opportunity to develop a market there which would be of great importance in the future.
I have been told this by fruit exporters and I got this second hand from them, but I understand that the rates presently charged by the Canadian National, shall I say, are such that it would be cheaper to haul the apples by truck all the way up to Amherst. Moncton and across New Brunswick and into the New England states rather than taking the apples across by boat.
If this matter were referred to the Canadian National perhaps they would consider adopting lower rates for the fall and winter months. The boat is going to be crossing anyway and it will cost the same to operate it whether or not it is loaded. Seasonal rates are a recognized procedure amongst common

carriers and if lower rates were put into effect this year it would substantially reduce the deficit, and would materially assist the agricultural industry of Nova Scotia and particularly the fruit growing industry, and it might also help to develop a future market in New England and be more satisfactory all the way round.

Mr. Chairman, I would just like to say a few words concerning the points raised by my hon. friend. The first two points I shall certainly draw to the attention of the Canadian National. I had heard something along the same lines of the remarks made by the hon. member concerning tickets and reservations but unfortunately I had not received any information as to what the situation really is.
With regard to the question of trucks I would just like to point out to the hon. member that we are still in a period of experiment. We have not yet had a complete 12 months' period of operations.
Earlier in the year I gave some consideration to having a seasonal rate for trucks, but after careful consideration we came to the conclusion that we should not inaugurate the seasonal rates at the present time but should give consideration to the matter when we had finished one year's operation of the vessel. I shall draw these points to the attention of the management and I hope it will be possible to deal with them satisfactorily.

Although the decision may have been made, I should like again to impress upon the minister the fact that there is an abnormal situation this year because of the possibility of substantial movements of fruit into New England and as far as the New York and Virginia markets. Perhaps the minister could take that into consideration.

Item agreed to.
468. To authorize the governor in council to grant to the government of the province of British Columbia a subsidy of $25,000 per mile, but not exceeding 50 miles, towards the construction of a line of railway of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway northward from Prince George in the province of British Columbia: such grant of subsidy to be made in such manner and in such amounts and subject to such conditions, if any, as the governor in council deems expedient; estimated requirement for the fiscal year 1956-57, $500,000.

I should like to make a few observations. The committee will recall that the government has offered $25,000 per mile for 50 miles in the construction of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway going north from Prince George. You will also recall that the department of Northern Affairs and National Resources was set up, put emphasis on the

north country, and that, of course, means that we must look forward to more transportation in that area.
It is my understanding that the British Columbia government has made an extensive survey of that northern area. The object, of course, is for the promotion of a railway going north into the Yukon and on into Alaska. I think the government would be wise to avail itself of any information that could be gathered from that survey and to get a real look at the prospects for this Pacific Great Eastern Railway.
It was interesting to note that the Prince George Citizen, in an article the other day, said that on August 2 the President of the United States signed a bill for an international rail and highway commission to look into the prospects of building a railway to Alaska.
I think that this emphasizes the importance that is being placed on the rail connection from Vancouver into Alaska. There is news coming out of the north that there are 100,000 square miles of oil leases in the Yukon, which would naturally indicate that there is going to be a great deal of work going on in that area in the prospecting for oil. There has been a new oil strike in Muckman pass, south of Dawson Creek, which apparently is going to have a bearing on the activity in that area.
The pipe line going south from Fort St. John has now reached the stage where we have 150 miles of the pipe already welded, and this means that it is not going to be long before the scrubbing plant at Fort St. John will be in the production stage of the by-products, which is going to mean an additional amount of freight originating in that area, for the two train loads of sulphur that are expected to be released from that plant every week will be carried over the Pacific Great Eastern Railway to the pulp mills in southern British Columbia.
There has been an outstanding increase of activity and population all through that northern area. The figures in the census just completed will show a sharp rise in population and economic growth generally. This again points to the fact that this railway is of the utmost importance, with the development that is taking place in that area today, to say nothing of the development that has taken place over the years.
There is another factor as well, I think, that should be taken into account. For the past two years this railroad has made a profit for the first time in its history. I think that is indicative too of the necessity for pushing the railroad north into the Peace river country. When it is pushed through to the
Supply-Transport
Peace river country, it is evident that it will save the Canadian taxpayers money because there are going to be less carloads of subsidized freight-grain-going 1,400 miles over the present road to Vancouver. It will only need to travel 700 miles. Naturally when freight is subsidized only for 700 miles instead of 1,400 miles, there will be effected a great saving of the taxpayers' money.
We have no figures available for the northern Alberta railroad to show what the freight out of that area is. The question is asked on page 2011 of Hansard, and the answer given shows that the dominion bureau of statistics has no figures relative to the freight carried out of that area. It will be recalled that I put three questions on the order paper, and it was found that the federal government had no statistics whatever as to the potential of the Peace river country, as far as freight or any other potential is concerned. I did not look it up, but that too may be found by looking in the index of Hansard.
In conclusion I should like to say that I think it is about time the government moved to clear itself in respect of the ridiculous position in which it has found itself in offering the amount of $25,000 per mile for only the first 50 miles of the railroad. Anyone who goes into that area and sees the tremendous expansion will certainly say that the figure just not does not make sense.

I should like to say a few words on this particular item because in my opinion the government is not acting fairly with regard to this subsidy. It was announced in the House of Commons by the Prime Minister on June 3 last year, at the same time that he announced a subsidy to aid in the construction of the line from Chibougamau to St. Felicien in the province of Quebec. In dealing with the subsidy to the Pacific Great Eastern Railway in British Columbia, the Prime Minister endeavoured to justify the limitation of the assistance to 50 miles on the ground that there was some timber 50 miles north of Prince George and, whilst the government felt that it would be economic to build that far, it was not prepared to subsidize into the Peace river, which is a total of 271 miles from Prince George. The Prime Minister also said that in later years, if there should be some change in the situation, the government might have another look.
I point out to the minister that the admitted purpose has been to get a railway into the Peace river district so that there will be an outlet from that area to the Pacific coast by a direct route rather than having to go back to Edmonton and then from Edmonton either to Prince Rupert or to Vancouver, which is

Supply-Transport
the case at the present time. The present Minister of Fisheries dealt with this situation very clearly in 1949. At that time the government was paying a subsidy of $15,000 a mile for the extension of this same Pacific Great Eastern Railway from Quesnel to Prince George, a distance of approximately 80 miles. The Minister of Fisheries, in speaking on that question, warned the government very convincingly that the fact that they were making this payment at that time must be considered as assuming the obligation to subsidize a railway to the Peace river. I have the discussion here. His statement will be found at page 1450 of Hansard for November 4, 1949. The important words which I wish to stress are these:
. . . when we are passing this appropriation I think we should be fully aware of all the implications, since we are committing ourselves to a policy of subsidizing the extension of this provincial railway.
Actually that was the situation in 1949 and it is the situation today. This subsidy should be made available for the whole extension into the Peace river district. I am not arguing at the moment anything about a subsidy to Alaska because that is not a practical question at the present time. But this line is no good at all if it only goes 50 miles north of Prince George. It has to go from Prince George through to the Peace river. The present Minister of Transport himself said last year, as found at page 6516 of Hansard of July 21:
As soon as we have further Information and further representations from the British Columbia government the matter will be re-examined and reconsidered.
That was a year ago and yet we find that the vote in the present estimates is only $500,000 which covers, I think, a subsidy for 20 miles. The vote last year involved a subsidy covering 10 miles, and it was only $250,000. I believe the government must face the fact that this whole extension should be subsidized. When the Minister of Fisheries spoke in 1949 there was a coalition government in power in British Columbia. I am not suggesting that influenced his views-
It certainly did not.

-or made any difference in his remarks but it certainly looks to me, as a neutral between the provincial government and the federal government, that one reason this subsidy is not being made available for the whole line is that there is now a Social Credit government in the province of British Columbia. I certainly do not believe it is possible for the minister to justify limiting this subsidy to the first 50 miles and I do not think it is possible for him to justify a refusal

to pay a subsidy on the whole extension when he is paying a subsidy on the whole extension in the province of Quebec.
I am not quarrelling for a minute with the subsidy for the line in Quebec. I think it is very appropriate. As a matter of fact, I think I was the first member in the house to insist that the line from Chibougamau to St. Felicien should be completed right away rather than being left in the air while the western half of the new line, that is, from the west into Chibougamau, was to be built. The original intention of the C.N.R. and of the government was that they would only build the line from the west, I think from Beattyville into Chibougamau, but as a result of pressure brought to bear in the house and by the residents of the Lake St. John area the government finally moved to build the whole line, including the eastern half from Chibougamau to St. Felicien.
I cannot see on what grounds the government can now refuse to grant this subsidy for the whole extension from Prince George into the Peace river area. I would ask the minister to tell the committee whether there has been any further consideration given to this subject and what the policy of the government is at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, we will talk
about the Chibougamau situation when we come to the next item. I do not want the hon. gentleman to walk off with the paternity of that branch line in the way he has just done but we might talk about that subject when we get to the next item. Hon. members will probably recall that last year the government announced, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has just said, simultaneously with the announcement concerning the Beattyville-Chibougamau-St. Felicien branch line, its intention to provide a subsidy at the rate of $25,000 a mile for the Chibougamau line and also for an extension not exceeding 50 miles in' length northward from Prince George of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway.
At that time the government was convinced from the information which had been placed before it and information which was already in its possession that it was doubtful whether an extension beyond 50 miles would be economic, and when I say "economic" I am thinking not in the strict interpretation of the word, that is to say, entirely self-supporting with a subsidy of $25,000 a mile. Because we believed on the information we then had that the 50 miles would be economic whereas a much greater extension would promise not to be economic, we limited our offer of assistance to 50 miles and to a sum of $25,000 a mile, which is the largest

amount of subsidy in recent years at least the problem. If not and if the hon. gentleman that has been paid by the government in wants to put further questions to me, I shall respect of any project.	try to answer them.

It is the same figure as the
Quebec subsidy.

Yes, but it is in fact the
largest amount of subsidy per mile applying to any project in recent years, and I would say perhaps for a good many years. We discussed this question of the P.G.E. subsidy last year. The hon. member of the Social Credit party who spoke just a moment ago spoke in rather glowing terms of the P.G.E. and its prospects but it seemed to me that his argument was rather contradictory in this sense. Mr. Chairman-

Perhaps if the hon. gentleman will let me finish he may find it will not be necessary to put his question. When we discussed the matter last year representations were made during the discussion that we should go farther than merely 50 miles, and so we ourselves asked the government of British Columbia to submit further facts, figures and information as to their own survey of the prospects of this particular region. The hon. member for Cariboo spoke a moment ago of the fact that the dominion bureau of statistics did not have any statistics for this area. I am sure he will realize it is not a matter of statistics but rather a matter of prospects. It is a projection of possibilities, an evaluation of what the future may hold.
We asked the provincial government to supply additional information. I say this by no means as criticism but merely as a statement of fact. It took the government of the province a long time to submit information to us in order for us to take a second look at this whole question. I should like to tell the members of the committee that we have gone very thoroughly into the further representations that were made by the province after considerable delay, and that the subject of providing an increase in subsidy-that is to say making it applicable to a greater extent of line than 50 miles-is under consideration at the present time. I do not want to express any final opinion in the matter because the matter has not yet come before cabinet. However, I do not exclude the possibility of a subsidy being provided for a greater length of line than 50 miles. I hope I have dealt with the significant aspects of

I hope the government is considering a subsidy for the whole of the remaining mileage to the Peace river and not merely say for another 50 miles, making a total of 100 miles that has been subsidized. As I pointed out in my earlier remarks, this is not a railway to go 50 miles or 100 miles north of Prince George. The railway does not make sense at all unless it goes through to the Peace river, and it should be treated on that basis. I hope the further subsidy which is being considered by the government is a subsidy on the whole of the 271 miles rather than on only a limited portion of that gap between Prince George and the Peace river.

I should like to offer one word of explanation with regard to a railway being profitable and asking for a subsidy. Even if the railroad is a profitable scheme, and if it is going to save the Canadian taxpayers money-and it certainly is going to do so,-*
It never will do so.

-I fail to see why the Canadian government should not participate in it. It is like your senior citizen's pension without a means test. Everybody gets it whether they have money or not. In the cafeteria, even though I have $5 in my pocket, I pay the same price as does the fellow who has a dollar in his pocket. There is no question about it at all; it is a matter of principle.

I cannot admit the suggestion that it was the pressure either from the hon. gentleman or from members of the opposition that led to the government decision in that connection. which the opposition claims the credit for all that the government does.

That is a very nice political speech, Mr. Chairman. The minister was not a member of this house when this question first came up. I am not particularly interested in getting credit or not getting credit. The Hansard record will speak for itself.

When that bill came up for second reading I pointed out that if only the western half of the line were built, the result would probably be that the business from Chibougamau would be turned into the Toronto area, and I urged very strongly that the eastern end of the line to Lac St. Jean should be built at the same time. On item 469, Mr. Chairman, before we dispose of the railway services item, I have a few remarks to make. I should like to ask him a question with regard to the Northern Alberta Railway. This railway serves directly the northern part of my constituency. My constituents are rather concerned about the fact that the railway, after about 25 or 30 years, is still under construction. Being under construction after that period of time has elapsed means only that this is a device for limiting service and increasing the freight rate. For some years that might have been something that you could justify because it was regarded as a fur trade route that had served for Mackenzie and so on, but those days have disappeared.

Mr. Chairman-
I have one or two remarks that I should like to make on this.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for York West.
I intend to talk about competition, but I did not know I was going to meet it so quickly.
You have a monopoly now.

There will be a monopoly for a few minutes, that is quite true. As a matter of fact I had prepared my notes for these remarks as long ago as March 16 and I have now had about six days of silent waiting so far as these estimates are concerned. Actually, I do not know whether this is a good day to talk about competition anyway because we seem to be facing competition with Marilyn Bell and the democratic national convention, so we find it fairly hard going right here.
I am not going to repeat what I have said before in connection with the overall competition picture in so far as our air services are concerned. As a matter of fact, I feel that the case for competition has been made out very well by several speakers in the house and certainly has been made out before the agency set up by the government to consider such matters, the air transport board. I should like to say, however, that the theory of competition in air transport matters deals with the protection of air routes and not with the protection of companies. I think that the whole idea is to ensure that a particular air route is allowed to develop so that adequate service may be obtained to any point on the route and it is not designed specifically for the protection of a company. Once it is assured that the particular areas in Canada do have adequate air transportation, then I think it is time that we looked at the position of the companies involved as to whether it might be possible to widen the scope of the service by the introduction of other air lines.
This particular matter, as it affects the whole industry from top to bottom, has been referred to in the press almost constantly over the last two or three years. As a matter of fact, two very able writers for our daily newspapers, Allan Kent of the Telegram and Muriel Snyder of the Globe and Mail, have,
Supp ly-Transport
in a series of articles, set out very adequately the present position of the case for competition. I might refer to just a few remarks that they have made by reading perhaps a sentence or so out of each of the articles as we go along.
Here is one which says:
Consider the plight of the general manager of a laundry whose president insists he must use washboards and not washing machines-all because the president is interested in developing a washboard factory.
This reference, of course, is to the fact that the government owned air line was saddled with tourist class equipment long after the leading air lines in the United States were able to have much more up to date equipment.
Here is a second little paragraph which says:
Trade Minister C. D. Howe's determination to protect T.C.A. against competition wherever possible is depriving Toronto of the status of an international air terminus.
Here is another one:
A beautiful dream-quite an intriguing one, though some people thought it impractical-was outlined last December to the air transport board who promptly shattered it.
It was a plan to inaugurate an inter-city aerobus service across Canada from Halifax to Vancouver,
which would be something like street car service_
you d just hop aboard the next one to come along.

Will the hon. member permit a question? Is he personally in favour of the kind of service that Pacific Air Lines was talking about and which is covered by the newspaper clippings to which he just referred?
I would think that is an unfair question.
I will withdraw it, then.

I would think the question to be determined is what type of company should provide the competition, and that should be decided by the agency set up to consider such problems. I think it is well established that within government policy the air transport board is that governmental agency. I do not believe we here should decide that any particular company or any particular plan should be the one when such an agency exists.
I might go on to answer the minister by saying this, that the attitude of the government has been such that it would discourage almost any operator from making such an application to the air transport board. It might be wise, in view of the lapse of time since we had the air freight hearing in Ottawa, for the board, under its terms of reference, to hold a hearing to determine at this time whether competition on a national

Supply-Transport
basis should be permitted. I might say that I am not exactly sure that the overall competition picture may require one service from coast to coast. It may be that there are secondary air companies which could provide this service on the basis of Winnipeg to Vancouver and another one from Halifax to Winnipeg. It may be that such competition now may consist of only two or three flights during the week during peak load periods. There appears to be a lack of space at peak load periods which could be taken care of without any detrimental effect to the government owned air lines.
I am not going to read the rest of these articles because apparently the minister does not find them too pleasant to listen to. I might say that one of them referred to the fact that someone had suggested in the house that perhaps we might even dispose of the government owned air lines to private interests. I think perhaps the writer was referring to the hon. member for York West. He asks who would buy it, principally because he says the return on the money is not great enough to interest investors. He points out that on a comparative basis the net return on the invested capital in comparison with other world operating air lines is very low. I am quite sure there would be an adequate number of people here in Canada quite prepared to invest in this type of enterprise. I might point out that there was an article in the Telegram just the other day which said that K.L.M., the Royal Dutch Air Lines, is prepared to issue common stock to the public and some may be sold in North America. So far as I recall, Mr. Chairman, this is a government owned air line and here is a situation where even Canadians may have an opportunity of buying into this company. I would suggest that there are plenty of patriotic Canadians interested in our air development who would be ready to take advantage of the opportunity to invest.
I may say I am pleased to see the Minister of Trade and Commerce has entered the chamber because I am speaking about one of his particular babies and perhaps my remarks should be addressed to him and not the Minister of Transport. There is another phase I should like to speak about in connection with competition and that is the international picture which is now developing. I believe that the gateway principle, in so far as international aviation is concerned, is going to be as dead as the dodo, the same as the steam locomotive. If we are going to pursue a policy of attempting to funnel international traffic by our own government controlled air lines into a particular port for embarkation overseas, then we are going to
[Mr. Hamilton (York West) .1
hold back the progress of international air travel in this country. It would appear that is the line we are presently taking. The Canadian Pacific Air Lines had great difficulty in reaching a stage where they could carry out overseas operations from Vancouver.
I know someone will say it is the international air transport association that effects and supervises the rates in connection with that transportation, but we have the situation -and I presume it is subscribed to and agreed to by our own national government air carrier-that even if you fly 1,500 miles less to go to Europe by Canadian Pacific Air Lines, you will have to pay the same fare that you would pay if you flew from Vancouver to Montreal and flew from there overseas. If that type of attitude is going to be carried out, as I say, it will minimize our chances of being in the forefront of international air travel development.
The same situation concerns our companies in connection with other runs; that is, the narrow point of view that we may lose eight or 10 passengers a week from Windsor to Toronto who take a trip to Mexico city prevents our international and other international carriers from landing in Windsor as well as in Toronto. Surely, that type of flight should be permitted to land in Windsor, Toronto and Montreal and surely the fortunes of our national air carrier service are not so tightly squeezed that they cannot stand losing the number of persons who once or twice a week travel between those cities to catch an international air carrier.
That was part of the agreement with the Mexican government. That was a condition imposed by the Mexican government, not by ourselves.
I would say this, Mr. Chairman. Probably this government did not waste any too much effort in ensuring that those stops were asked for and obtained in an international agreement.

Will the hon. gentleman permit me to interrupt him on that point? I am just going to ask him this question. As between Canadian Pacific Air Lines flying between Windsor and Mexico and the Mexican air lines flying from Windsor to Mexico, which line would the hon. gentleman use?
I do not know whether this question has anything to do with what I am saying, but I am quite satisfied that I would use Canadian Pacific Air Lines.

That was just exactly what the Mexican government thought. If the competition were between the two air lines from

between the same two points, Windsor to Mexico city, their air line would not get the business.

I am quite sure that with respect to the Mexican air line- if they have a minister of transport, and I know they have because I have been down there-if the minister of transport were asked the same question he would get the same answer, namely, that those who are flying from Mexico in all likelihood would have a preference for flying on his air line. Surely, if both carriers were accorded this privilege the public would have the advantage. Now, these particular observations apply not only to Toronto but apply, and will apply in the future, to cities like Winnipeg which at the present time might be able to have the advantage of direct service to Europe, which they have not at the present time.
In the foreseeable future, direct service will be available from the major cities in Canada, or should be available, if this government sees the light, for people to travel directly to Europe. When I say "direct service" I can easily see it happening to Edmonton. Certainly, I think it could be made available almost immediately there. It could be made available to Calgary and to cities of that kind. If we are looking ahead I do believe it is time that we dropped the gateway principle in so far as our international air traffic is concerned.

Mr. Chairman,
I am having a very busy time with the government benches. No, I do not think I would let it drop into any city. I do not see any necessity for that question. I believe the traffic potential will be there. The question of how many lines are required to serve that particular potential may be surveyed by your agency and determined at that time whether it is ready to absorb, or at least fill, the demand for the service.
