I might ask the minister this. Does he not see the time in the future when one will take off from Chicago or Detroit and fly directly to Europe,
Supply-Transport
and when one will take off in Toronto and fly directly to Europe? Does he not see that in the future as far as he is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, I would not think so; no.

Well, then, I should say that the minister's optimism which is usually quite apparent in this house does not apply in the particular instance where it affects his government-owned airline which he has brought along, and I may say brought along very well, from infancy; but surely we are not going to pull down our sights at this stage and end it there.
Perhaps I might be allowed to go on. I think I have built up a fair case in the past on precedent and on quoting cases. I am not going to do that today, but I should like to repeat, if I may, the Prime Minister's words, dealing with competition in the air field. This is what he said before the air industries and transportation association in November, 1953, at which time there was no decision yet in the application for a competitive air freight system.
I will assure you that the government does not necessarily intend to guarantee every operator a permanent monopoly in his area.
Let me assure you that whichever way the decision goes now-
And he was referring to the Canadian Pacific Air Lines case.
it will not in the long run be a decision in favour of perpetuation of monopoly conditions. I have stated many times, before representatives of other industries that the government to which I belong believes that as a general rule the public can be best served under competitive conditions. And I believe that once the air transport industry is soundly established, the decisions to be made by any Canadian government should be in favour of opportunities for competition.
And in view of the tremendous development of our resources that has been taking place, a development which shows no sign of relenting, the demands for the services of commercial aircraft should increase to such an extent that increase in competition will be both desirable and beneficial.
I do not think I have to look any further for an authority in connection with this situation than the Prime Minister of this country, Mr. Chairman, and I ask again, as I have asked before, have we not reached the stage in our development covered by the quotation I have just read?
This particular feature does not simply affect the operation of a couple of air companies. Clamping down on competition at the top is felt right through the industry. If one has travelled through the north country he will have seen that there has been a foreclosure to a great extent on the expansion of adequate air services. Of course, if we are to have this service we have to improve our airports. I know the minister has said that

Supply-Transport
conditions in Europe are different. They may have one major airport in a country and that is all they have to worry about and they are really doing a nice job on it; whereas we have 3,000 miles and many airports to look after. But I for one find little excuse for the condition, as an example, in which we find the Malton airport today. I have articles here which say that agreements are being reached and that plans are going ahead. As a matter of fact, Malton is a disgrace to the city of Toronto. The airport facilities there are entirely inadequate, and the plans which are being undertaken now to push out a few partitions leave conditions still in the position where people are being herded in and herded out like cattle. In addition, I may say, even the washrooms are a disgrace. It does not matter what time of the day you go there, they are never clean. I do not blame the contractor, if there is a contractor on the job. I simply say the facilities are so inadequate that it would be almost impossible to do anything about them.
When I read a heading in the Telegram about what we are looking forward to, about Malton being one of the great airports of the world-that is, provided we can have the Minister of Trade and Commerce raise his sights a bit-if we are getting ready for that stage then I should say we certainly are not making very rapid progress.
There is one other matter I would like to speak about before I sit down and that is the question of over-all safety. Very seldom now does one leave a civil airport without hearing the whine of jet aircraft in one's ears. I noticed an article not too long ago which gave an indication that jet military aircraft were not going to be allowed to operate from civilian airports. When I asked the minister about it in the house I was informed that there were no plans concerning this.
I think people should realize we are entering a new stage in air transport development when we can talk about jet military aircraft and super constellations in the same area that may be approaching each other at the same speed as a Colt automatic bullet. It takes at least three miles for a pilot to be able to see the image and transfer it into action by avoiding danger that might be involved.
In addition to this we have had two investigations in the United States which have disclosed that there is an indication that the turbulence set up from the wing tips and jet engines of jet aircraft constitutes a great danger to lighter types of planes. The boards of inquiry have come to the conclusion in two cases that the only explanation is that getting into such a situation has resulted either in complete loss of control of the aircraft or disintegration of the plane itself.

I think there was some indication of that happening in the Toronto area in the loss of an Otter aircraft not too long ago.
I would suggest, sir, that consideration be given immediately to the separation of military and civilian aircraft at civilian airports. This may not mean a great expense because we have a great many unused airfields some of which are in commuting distance of our major cities. With car travel as it is today it would be possible to commute back and forth.
As far as the safety situation is concerned I believe that in Washington they are presently working on a reduced speed plan not just in the immediate airport area, which I understand to be within three or five miles, but in the general area of about 30 miles, and they are extending their landing pattern to that extent. I understand that good results have been obtained in Washington as a result of this reduction in speed. It appears to me that something of that nature is necessary over and above the separation of flying heights which has been the plan of the department and by which certain aircraft fly above 9,500 feet. In fact, I do not think this alone will overcome the real danger which exists in the airport areas.
One matter which comes to mind in connection with the dangers of the situation is the matter of investigations of accidents. I am not going into a lengthy discussion of what the Canadian pilots association has charged plane operators and the government with or the answers that were obtained, but I think it is notable that in one case partial responsibility was placed on the department. As I understand it, this was the only occasion on which an outside party has been appointed as a member of the board of inquiry.
In many instances we do not appear to receive any answer as to the reason for these accidents although the R.C.A.F. has a good record as far as investigations are concerned. I understand they are able to trace down the cause of the accidents in almost 90 per cent of the cases.
I think that in the future if there is an indication that the operator is at fault there should be a new method of assessing the situation and conducting the investigation. A board of inquiry might include an officer from the R.C.A.F., a member from the Department of Transport and an outside party as well. If this procedure were followed it seems to me we would be able to leave a better taste in the public's mouth concerning the findings of many of these investigations.
In conclusion I would repeat that I am hoping the vision the Minister of Trade and

Commerce displayed in 1937 and 1938 will not be restricted in 1956. We are on the threshold of great developments in the air transport field and at one time this country was rated No. 1 in this regard. With the great stretches of territory we have in Canada it is most essential that rapid development take place here. I hope we lift our sights and insure that we will soon be in the top spot again.

Mr. Chairman, I merely want to obtain some information. I agree with what was said by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat concerning the fact that the pattern of air travel is changing rapidly and it is in connection with this change in pattern that I would like to get some information from the minister.
As the minister is aware, the airport at Sydney is one of the main stations for the overseas trade. Most of the ships from Europe, England and many from the United States returning from Europe use that port. It is pretty busy all the time.
I observed an item in the press this morning to the effect that T.C.A. proposes to put into service a larger jet ship which would carry 120 passengers. In view of such developments I am wondering about the adequacy of this particular airport to retain its place of importance in the overseas trade.
The runways at that station are about 8,000 feet in length and I am informed it will require a runway at least 4,000 feet longer than that to accommodate the type of aircraft that it is proposed will be in use in the not far distant future.
My reason for raising the matter at this time and seeking to obtain information from the minister is that this is a question which has been agitating the board of trade in the Sydney area for some considerable time. They have been in touch with the department with a view to ascertaining if it is the plan of the minister's department to make any extensions or renovations at that airport.
In the same connection there is another matter I would like to mention. The passenger building at that airport is an old converted hangar. The general set-up there is, I think, as good as any in Canada; certainly it is better than the airport at Malton or Dorval. The service and catering are both good. They are able to handle the immigrants arriving at that station very expeditiously. However, the roof on that old hangar is nearly as high as the roof of this chamber and the old roof girders are exposed. It would not be an expensive job to cover up that overhead mess. The fact that it is uncovered means that the building is cold
Supply-Transport
and drafty in the winter months and it is difficult to work under those conditions.
I took the matter up with the minister's predecessor on several occasions and I thought I almost had it nailed down, but Mr. Chevrier went on to other work. Is the minister in a position to give me any information as to whether there are any plans with respect to the expansion of the airways and the renovation of that station and is he prepared at least to think about doing something about what is a very bad sight?

If I might deal with the question the hon. member for Cape Breton South just raised, I should like to tell him in a general way that the introduction of jet aircraft is unquestionably going to thrust upon us a very considerable burden in the matter of the extension of runways at a great many airports in Canada. If I were not optimistic in my outlook, I might be somewhat oppressed by the magnitude of the expenditures that seem to be in prospect. But I think the hon. member will agree that these difficulties in anticipation are always greater than they are seen to be when we are faced with reality.
Bearing that fact in mind, I am not discouraged or oppressed by the magnitude of the expenditures that unquestionably we shall have to make in order to meet the changed conditions that jet aircraft are going to bring about. Having that principal thought in mind, I am quite sure that the hon. member will agree with me that we must place the emphasis first on the essential facilities, and by that I mean runways and facilities for safety in the air, rather than on what I might describe as conveniences.
The hon. gentleman has referred to the terminal building in Sydney, which I know, though not nearly as well as he does. I can think of several places in Canada that would be quite happy if we could transport the building at Sydney and place it elsewhere.
I am quite appreciative of the fact that the people of Sydney would not care for the idea, but the building is by no means a bad building, and I would doubt very much if I should hold out any real hope of making any substantial change to the building in the near future. I am quite sure that members of the committee will agree with me that the emphasis must be on the facilities for the aircraft themselves, so as to make air travel possible, rather than on providing excellent terminal facilities.
Before I leave that subject, I should like to say that very recently we initiated discussions with T.C.A. as to the works which they believe will be necessary in order to

Supply-Transport
meet their program of expanded services and at the same time to meet the different operating conditions that will be created when we have jet aircraft, when we have to increase the number of points served by Viscount aircraft and when we consider particularly the places that will be served by these long-range jet aircraft. Those discussions are going to be resumed very shortly, but I will say that there will be an extensive program of work to be carried out.
Now I come back to the question of competition, which the hon. member for York West mentioned in his remarks. I am not going to try to deal with the subject quite as fully as he has done. I am quite ready to admit that there is much to be said for those who argue in favour of competition but I do not think that those who are arguing for competition are being realistic about the matter. I think their arguments are based primarily on theoretical considerations and do not take account of the realities of the situation in Canada.
I know that the hon. gentleman knows full well that it is quite difficult, looking across the whole field of national and international aviation, to find countries where there are truly competitive services. We know, of course, that in Europe there are competitive services between points such as London and Paris, London and Zurich, Athens and Rome, and one could go on multiplying the examples very easily, but when you look into those cases you find that the so-called competition exists because the service was established as a result of a bilateral agreement between the two countries concerned. Each country, quite naturally and quite properly, was interested in providing its service through its national airlines so that it could share with the airline of the other country concerned the business that was there to be developed.
However, though I have looked very carefully to find examples that would seem to justify the opinions of those who believe that we should have competition of the same kind in Canada, I cannot say that I have succeeded in finding any example that seems to me to have any very real merit. I do not want to bore the members of the committee with a lot of figures, but when one examines the volume of traffic carried between, let us say, the European capitals or between important cities in the United States where there are these competitive services, we find that they are so much greater than anything we have in Canada that they invalidate entirely the arguments in favour of competition in Canada right across the country.

I am going to give just a few figures. I have not the figures for 1955, but in the case of the service between London and Paris in 1954 the total number of passengers carried was 415,000. As far as I can make out, that is the biggest of the intercity services in Europe. Let us look at some of the figures in the United States. Between New York and Chicago there are four major airlines operating services. When you look at the total of their figures you find that in 1954 these four lines between them carried 541,600 passengers. Between New York and Boston, another service where there is heavy traffic, three airlines divide up the business, and there were 534,600 passengers in 1954. Between Montreal and New York, a service which was divided between Colonial and T.C.A., there were 166,700.
We have no service in Canada that comes anywhere near to approaching those figures.
I have figures here for the passengers between Toronto and Montreal. I do not think it includes people who would be travelling from Montreal to Toronto and on to Winnipeg, but it gives a good idea of the volume of business between Montreal and Toronto. In 1954 the total was 101,000. Here we have an example of the two cities between which the traffic is at the highest point, and the total is only slightly in excess of 100,000, whereas, as I pointed out, the London-Paris service is over 400,000, the New York-Chicago and the New York-Boston each over 500,000.
I am not trying to argue that it would not be possible in theory to establish competitive services between Montreal and Toronto but I think it is foolish to consider only this one rather small aspect of the whole problem. What is important is that as Canadians we should take an over-all view of the situation. If we do that we can reasonably say to a nationally owned line: We want you to provide a transcontinental service and we want you to provide other services which are not inherently paying and are not inherently economic. I do not believe we can expect that to be done if we are going to say the field is open, anybody can compete, and whoever can stand the competition wins out.
May I be permitted a question?
Certainly.

I do not think we have suggested that just anybody should come into the picture. Would the minister answer this question. If we have eight transcontinental flights today and it becomes apparent that two more are needed, would there be any detrimental effect on the

nationally owned air line if one other operator, no matter whom it might be, were permitted to handle those two extra flights?

I suppose it is a question of degree. It seems to me that when one looks at it in the abstract one might be inclined to say that it would not make any difference, but I think when you come down to examining it you will find that the moment you establish two air lines you must immediately establish two ground organizations, and when you establish two ground organizations then, I think, you have ultimately to divide the business between the two operators. When you do that you come to the point inevitably, I think, that both cannot operate at a profit, which means that you have a choice between competition and a subsidy on the one hand or the kind of thing we have now with service at cost to the Canadian people.
I think that is the essence of the matter, and quite candidly I believe that the policy we are now following with respect to T.C.A. is conducive to the development of civil aviation in the best interests of Canadians. I cannot believe that competition can have any other effect than that of raising the cost to Canadians either through higher fares or through the necessity of providing subsidies to keep the operators going.
How does the minister reconcile his closing sentence with the statement made by the Prime Minister three years ago?

I have read what the Prime Minister has said, not only on the occasion to which the hon. gentleman referred but on other occasions, and I did not find anything in what the Prime Minister has said that suggested that any time in particular had been fixed when competitive services would be instituted. When the Prime Minister spoke in the house on November 16, 1953, on the question of competitive services he quoted what Professor Curtis, I believe, had said on the subject and I do not see any harm, even if it does take a minute, in putting on the record again the words the Prime Minister cited. The Prime Minister said that the matter had been put in a manner that had made some impression upon him, and then he quoted these words:
Competition is only useful for what it achieves. If it achieves greater efficiency, lower costs and charges and better service, it is an admirable principle to insist upon. But if it achieves overexpansion of expensive facilities with division of the market amongst competing carriers, it will lead to heavy burdens on carriers, shippers and taxpayers alike.
I do not think I can improve on that quotation, and I think it shows very clearly what was in the Prime Minister's mind at that time.
Supply-Transport

The minister's answer to my question was not very informative. I asked him a specific question with respect to a specific airport. Press dispatches I have seen would lead me to believe that the Sydney board of trade is afraid of the airport there being by-passed unless some renovations are made. I should like to ask the minister if there is any possibility of that happening.

I wish I were sufficiently
omniscient to be able to predict the future accurately. I think a great deal is going to depend on the pattern of flying that develops once jet aircraft go into operation. Their range and speed are so much greater than that of aircraft now flying the north Atlantic. They are talking, for instance, in the case of the DC-8 of a speed of 600 miles per hour, and I should not be at all surprised if we find, just as the hon. member for York West suggested a little earlier, that we may have flights leaving London and flying directly to Montreal without any intermediate stops.
What is perhaps more important is the situation at the moment in Sydney, and I do not hesitate to tell my hon. friend that Sydney is on the list of airports at which T.C.A. is asking us to do some work. I do not think it is contemplated that there should be a runway extension of 4,000 feet. I do not know how long the existing runways are, but I do not think it is contemplated that it should be quite as much as that.

Mr. Chairman, I must say that the arguments advanced by the minister in opposition to the need of competition for Trans-Canada Air Lines seemed to me to lack the cogency and logic usually exhibited by the minister. He seemed to be labouring at some length and with considerable diffidence to advance the argument that there would be no improvement in air service in the event that there was competition.
I do not think I said just that.
No, the minister may not have said quite just that. He contended that if there was opposition subsidies might be necessary.
If there was competition subsidies might be necessary.
Yes. He joins the two together.
Higher fares or subsidies.

It seems to me that argument is one that would be dissipated very shortly if an opportunity were given for competition. I am one who uses Trans-Canada Air Lines a great deal and I have a

Supply-Transport
high regard for the officials of that organization. I believe there would be a vast improvement in the service with competition because, human nature being what it is, an organization that has a monopoly over a service function such as Trans-Canada has does not exert diligence like that exerted by those who are subject to competition.
However, it was not that matter I rose to discuss for a moment. I wish to refer to the need for establishment across the northern areas of Canada of a freight or cargo line. So far as the western provinces are concerned, generally speaking Trans-Canada today serves the southern portions of those provinces. The minister will immediately say that Trans-Canada passes through Saskatoon. Saskatoon is at least 250 miles south of the centre of Saskatchewan. That gives one some indication of the fact that the concentration of Trans-Canada service is in the southern portions of the western provinces.
Two or three years ago an application was made on the part of Canadian Pacific Air Lines to permit the establishment of a regular freight or cargo service from Montreal to Winnipeg, thence through northern Saskatchewan, thence to Edmonton and finally to Vancouver. The development in the northern portions of the western provinces in recent years has been phenomenal. Anyone who has not visited northern Alberta, northern Saskatchewan or northern Manitoba has no conception of the mineral development that is taking place. Surely we in the western provinces, in those northern portions that deserve service, should not be denied cargo freight service when Trans-Canada Air Lines itself refuses to inaugurate such a system but adopts this attitude toward a competitor that is not asking for any subsidy but wants to establish a regular freight cargo transport service.
Where does the hon. gentleman mean with respect to this cargo service? Is it transcontinental or what?

As I recall it, the original application was from Montreal to Winnipeg or to The Pas, Prince Albert, Edmonton and then on to the coast. Trans-Canada Air Lines is denying the development that should be available in those northern portions of our country by adopting a dog in the manger attitude in this regard. It refuses to enter the field itself. Canadian Pacific Air Lines does not ask for any subsidy. It asks merely for the opportunity to perform a service that is necessary.
You mean they did ask. They are not asking now.
They what?
They did ask. They are not asking now.

Oh, that is not correct.
I say that with great deference. They asked the right to establish a line.
That is a question of the past but not of the present.

I am going to ask the
minister whether further application has been made. As I recall the matter, when they made their application two and a half or three years ago Trans-Canada Air Lines said "No, under no circumstances". We are being denied-I refer to Winnipeg; The Pas; Prince Albert; I am not so sure about North Battle-ford, whether it was to connect there or not; Edmonton and thence on to the coast-the freight cargo service for which there is available traffic sufficient to permit Canadian Pacific Air Lines to inaugurate it. However, it is faced by this monolithic organization that refuses to go into the field itself and stands in the position of guard against those who would.
The boards of trade throughout western Canada particularly have asked that something be done in this connection. There can be no justification for the holding back of advances in transportation on the bare supposition that some time Trans-Canada Air Lines will feel constrained to establish a government freight cargo service. I care not where one goes throughout western Canada, in every province there is a constant and continuing demand for service which is being denied. Because of that denial there is denied to vast areas the advancement and development that would otherwise take place.
When my hon. friend advances arguments in opposition to the establishment of a competitive passenger line, his arguments cannot in any way apply to a freight cargo line for which there is a demand; for which there have been repeated requests from boards of trade everywhere; and in respect of which mining corporations, expanding as they are, provide a fertile source of traffic. But Trans-Canada Air Lines stands as a guard against that development. It was never intended that so paradoxical a situation should be created that the creature of the government should deny expansion in this country because it stands, as it were, as a bulwark against private enterprise performing a proper, necessary and desirable function.
The minister says there has been some change in the application.
No, I did not say that.

Two years ago or thereabouts the Prime Minister said that reconsideration would be given to this question.

At that time he indicated that that reconsideration would not be far removed. We have now waited for a year and a half and there has been no change in so far as the public is concerned. I would ask the minister to explain why this situation should exist. With the vast developments that are taking place in my own province and which are making for a potential uranium production unequalled anywhere in the world; when in the neighbourhood of Lac la Ronge vast copper finds are being made; when in the neighbourhood of 60 miles northeast of Prince Albert a tremendous area is now being weighed with a view to ascertaining its potentialities as one of the great iron-producing areas of Canada outside of the Labrador area and the province of Quebec, when Trans-Canada Air Lines is unwilling to take the step which is so necessary, namely to inaugurate a freight cargo regular service, why should they not be willing to step aside and allow private enterprise to do it, whether it be Canadian Pacific Air Lines or another air line, whatever one is prepared to give the best service, and having regard to previous performance and financial reliability? Why is it that this service should not be permitted?
I would ask the minister to go into this question at some length, for it represents one of the major reasons-I refer to the failure to establish this service-that we in the western provinces find ourselves discriminated against in respect of freight rates to a degree that in other provinces of Canada would not be tolerated.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to take very much time to reply to the hon. gentleman, despite his invitation that I do so at length. The hon. gentleman's speech might well have been made in 1953; but the conditions in 1956 are not the same as those that existed in 1953. The hon. gentleman speaks of T.C.A. having refused to go into the field themselves. He says he does not care where the services go, that we should consider this application of Canadian Pacific Air Lines.
There is no application of Canadian Pacific Air Lines that is currently before the air transport board for a cargo service. The hon. gentleman knows that there was one in 1953, but that it was rejected. When an application is rejected, a new one must be made. No new application has been made. But the most significant fact that has escaped the hon. gentleman entirely is that there is daily- from Montreal to Toronto, to Winnipeg, to Edmonton and Vancouver-an all-cargo service operated by Trans-Canada Air Lines. I do not see how he can suggest that we should have another. The great difficulty about an 67509-4691
Supply-Transport
air cargo service is that the traffic is strictly one directional; it moves westward, but very' little moves eastward.
My own assessment of the situation, without having studied the figures with great care, is that there is enough for one, for one flight per day, but not for two. So far as the service to some of the other points the hon. gentleman mentioned is concerned, for the most part Trans-Canada services are east-west lateral services, whereas the private operators are carrying on, I think at some profit to themselves, operations in a north-south direction or vertically. How can the hon. gentleman suggest, when he already complains against the T.C.A. monopoly, that T.C.A. should invade these fields which are taken care of by private operators? All I can say, Mr. Chairman, is that the hon. gentleman has gone astray owing to the fact he does not know about this cargo service which is run daily.
I know about that, but that does not help us at all in the northern part.

I take it the hon. member for Prince Albert is also saying that somehow or other we should also have the Canadian Pacific in there. There is nothing to stop Canadian Pacific Air Lines from making an application. I doubt if they want to.

My hon. friend has removed himself from the ambit of my argument. I am speaking about the northern parts of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, thence to Vancouver, not about the southern part. The southern parts of those provinces are well served by T.C.A., but T.C.A. is not in the northern part; and because T.C.A. is not in the northern part we are asking, whether it be Canadian Pacific Air Lines or some other private corporation, that there be established a cargo freight line through the northern parts of those provinces.
Many of those points have service already, including C.P.A.
When the last application was made, you opposed it.
We are talking about the 1953 application, which was for an east-west service.

I am not speaking about north-south, I am speaking about east-west.
I mentioned Montreal to Winnipeg to Le Pas and so on through the northern portion to Vancouver. The minister said there has not been a recent application. The Prime Minister indicated that reconsideration was being given to the question and there might not be opposition.

Supply-Transport
When did the Prime Minister say that?

About a year and a half ago; it would be in May, 1955. I am glad to hear that suggestion. The minister says that no application has been made recently. A company is not going to make application knowing that it is going to be opposed and that the same result is going to be achieved which was achieved the last time. There is no use in an applicant, however worthy, butting its head against a stone wall of opposition. The air transport board will not consider the application if it is a matter of government policy that this northern route shall not be permitted for air cargo.
The minister says let us talk about the situation today. I give him an opportunity to talk about it. If an application were made now to the air transport board for a northern route, would the government take the same stand it did two and a half or three years ago and oppose it, or does the government intend to adopt a disinterested attitude in regard to such an application? That is bringing the question right up to date, and I thank the minister for suggesting it be brought up to date. What is the government's attitude now?

What the hon. member is suggesting is that I should decide now what might be the circumstances if Canadian Pacific Air Lines made an application to establish an east-west cargo service. First, in my opinion, it is very unlikely that Canadian Pacific Air Lines will ask for the right to carry cargo from Montreal across the country to Vancouver. I think they would have been very sorry if their application had been granted in 1953. I say wait until we see what is their appreciation of the present situation before I attempt to say what the government will do.

I have just one more question of the minister. What is government policy? You do not have to wait and see to know what government policy is. What is government policy now with reference to allowing a competing trans-Canada route for cargo transportation east and west which will not cover areas that are covered by Trans-Canada but will cover' areas that today are not receiving the attention they should receive in this regard? What is government policy today? If the minister will say that, then the whole thing is clarified. I was invited by him to bring it up to date, to 1956, and I am glad to do so. What is the policy now?

The hon. member for Prince Albert thinks he has just uncovered a gold mine here. I will not hesitate to answer his
flVBr. Diefenbaker.]
question if he will be more precise as to the points to be served; if we know what traffic is available and who is at present carrying it and where the traffic is to originate. Then we will have an opportunity of knowing at least what are the facts. If the hon. gentleman would like to have my opinion as to whether or not, on a transcontinental basis, there is enough business for two carriers, I would express the opinion that there is not. I do not think the government would encourage an applicant to try to divide what is not sufficient business for one carrier. I do not think it would make sense that we should have two carriers taking care of what is not enough for one.

I am very pleased, Mr. Chairman, that you were not able to see me a little sooner, because it has given me an opportunity to listen to a very excellent debate and, so to speak, make possible a very good preface for something I want to discuss. I am not perturbed by the troubles that are brought forth by the hon. member for York West and the hon. member for Prince Albert even though I am, as they are, interested in free enterprise. I have, like the hon. member for York West, attended the committees where we have discussed T.C.A. and all the relative factors. In view of this I have to go along with the minister, and I think he made a very able reply. I appreciated very much the quotation he gave in reply from the Prime Minister regarding air transport matters. I think that, in a brief way, covers what should be our aim in all air matters.
Just to show that I do subscribe to the free enterprise theory in some air transport matters I am going to register a complaint about air transport in the northern part of my riding, which extends into the province of Alberta. I think this complaint will fit into the delineation of the remarks of the Prime Minister as to what constitutes something that should be under free enterprise. This is very important to the area at Beaver-lodge and Uranium City which, over the past two years during the development of the uranium mines, has come into the air transport picture in a rather big way. I doubt very much if there is any place in Canada which continuously has an airlift of freight into it that this place has.
I want to talk about government policy with regard to air freight going into there and some of its detrimental effects as now constituted. I hope the minister will have a new look at this policy. I can see why it was instituted in the first place and maybe why it has been continued up to the present

time, but I think if the facts are considered now there may be some reason for changing the policy somewhat.
On July 19, 1955, an application was heard in Edmonton by the air transport board for a second air line to carry freight from Edmonton into Uranium City and the Beaverlodge area, roughly 400 miles. Under the original policy Canadian Pacific Air Lines were granted a sole charter into that area. I can quite recognize why that was good government policy in the first instance. It was a new and embryo country, particularly a new and embryo industry, and it was not known whether there was a lot of uranium there or maybe not quite so much. The main interest was to get a company which could perform a service in that area and would guarantee to maintain that service. Therefore I can see the point in making an agreement with a company such as Canadian Pacific Air Lines that was in a position to give that kind of service.
We have now had it for a period of three or four years, and in the light of our experience we can now see that it is a highly profitable proposition as far as Canadian Pacific Air Lines are concerned, or should be. The hon. member for Prince Albert mentioned subsidies to Canadian Pacific Air Lines. I can assure the committee that if all the lines are like that one we would not need much in the way of subsidies. They charge 12 cents a pound or $240 a ton from Edmonton to Uranium City.
At the hearing before the air transport board another line, I believe Associated Airways, wished to put freight over that same route northbound for 6 cents a pound, or just half the Canadian Pacific Air Lines' rate. Nothing was heard of that for some months, though I believe they made a pretty fair case before the air transport board. I believe the air transport board was considerably impressed, and thought this might be a good thing to grant. To this day you cannot tell the people in that area that it was a coincidence that there was a cabinet meeting on the morning of November 30, and the air transport board's decision was rendered that afternoon in a negative way.
I can assure the hon. gentleman that the cabinet does not have any power of review over the air transport board's decision. What the hon. gentleman is implying was a pure coincidence.

That is just exactly the interjection I wanted, to disabuse that idea in that area. I have been trying to disabuse it myself. I hope they will take the minister's
Supp ly-Transport
word where they would not take mine. However, this double air freight rate is charged there by, as you might say, government decree, because this other company was prepared to operate in there for $120 a ton or 6 cents a pound, compared with 12 cents a pound or $240 a ton charged by Canadian Pacific Air Lines.
There are other yardsticks to use to find out whether or not this can be done. In the recent committee on research I asked the chief of Atomic Energy and of all our uranium works, Mr. Bennett, why his Eldorado Company did not patronize Canadian Pacific Air Lines. He said, "It costs too much". That is exactly the answer I expected. If you examine Eldorado's operations you will find that they have been forced by this policy to put in their own air line, as other uranium companies have, if they are big enough to own an air line. Economics force them to do it, because no mining company wants to go into the air transport business. They are miners, and they want to stay in the mining business. Such companies as Gunnar have done that, and now because of this policy Lorado, which is building a big new plant for uranium production, are putting in their own air transport service.
I think if you will look into the operation of Eldorado's air arm you will find that they have been transporting their own goods at something in the neighbourhood of $100 a ton, or 5 to 5J cents a pound. They are not an air line exclusively; therefore the question might be asked as to whether they function just as smoothly and economically as a proper line would. This policy of agreeing to a certain rate, and theirs is $240 a ton, puts companies in this position. Lorado, I may say, went to Canadian Pacific Air Lines this year and asked whether they would give them a special rate if the mining company gave them all their business at the new mill going in. They said yes, they would give them a rate of $240 a ton, or 12 cents a pound, which is exactly what they charge all the companies. Another company was prepared to do it for half that, a sound company.
I believe other companies besides the one I just mentioned are prepared to go in and do it for half the rate charged right now. I think we can show that the air arm of the government's own company, Eldorado, are putting it in there for less than 6 cents a pound, but we must also keep in mind that they are allowed accelerated depreciation on their aircraft, and so on. Therefore I do not think it is going to be difficult to show that a second company could well make money at the 6 cents a pound or $120 a ton rate.

Supp ly-Transport
The man on the street up there who is not able to put in his own air line has to pay the Canadian Pacific Air Lines' rate. The fact is that practically all groceries and perishables have to go in by air, and the ordinary man on the street is compelled to pay 60 cents a quart for milk, for instance. This is an item that is a good example to everybody, because it brings home to everyone just what it means to that area. It is not the doubling of the truck rate or the doubling of the rail freight rate, which are peanuts compared with the doubling of the air freight rate. The average person thinks that if this other company had been allowed to go in and compete, milk would be 35 cents a quart instead of 60 cents.
I was happy to have the minister read the observations of the Prime Minister on this very point, because it gives me some ray of hope that this is not a permanent situation; that another look will be taken at it, and that is all I am asking. All I am asking is that it will be given another look, in view of all the factors. I think it can be proved that other companies can operate at a profit at the rate at which they said they could operate.
These are some of the reasons they should be able to operate at a profit. The picture is rapidly changing, particularly with respect to uranium shipments. It is quite likely that the Minister of Transport will have to confer with the Minister of Trade and Commerce, because they are both concerned in it. Uranium production is increasing very rapidly in that area. Gunnar is going to double the size of the plant it put in last year. The government's Eldorado plant is being tripled in size this year, and Lorado is putting in a brand new plant, with the result that for a little while we are going to have an effect something like the effect of iron ore itself on the St. Lawrence seaway. Within a little while the majority of freight is going to move up river on the St. Lawrence, with the advent of full production of iron ore.
With the advent of full production of uranium, which may take place in about 18 months, the southbound freight will exceed the northbound freight. These companies which are prepared to go in and cut the northbound freight rate in half are prepared to bring out the concentrate, as I understand it, and there will be a volume of between 20,000 and 40,000 pounds a day within the next year and a half or two years. They will have to pay something between 2 and 3 cents a pound.
I asked Mr. Bennett if he would be interested in prices of that sort, and he said definitely they would be. One thing disturbed him somewhat, and that was how they were

going to get the concentrate out of Great Bear lake, which is a separate operation; but I think that could be overcome all right through some free competition in that area. Whoever got the contract for hauling the concentrate out of Gunnar and Eldorado and these other places would, I think, give a fairly good rate on hauling it out of Great Bear as well.
I hope the government will take another look at this policy of maintaining the double air freight rate up there, because it is not a small consideration. This is an air freight rate and what results is that $120 is added to the cost of every ton of groceries and the necessities of life that go into that area; and this has been done by the decree of the present government. It has had the result that companies have had to put in their own air lines, whereas the ordinary working man up there cannot take advantage of the volume of freight that is going in. If there were competition everyone in that area could enjoy the advantages of this volume of freight that is moving up there.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Transport will get together with the Minister of Trade and Commerce and review this policy in the light of the facts I have mentioned, which can be easily ascertained and verified.

Mr. Chairman, I was quite interested in listening to the reply the minister made a while ago to the hon. member for Cape Breton South and in hearing him say that he intended to place the emphasis on providing facilities that will make travel by aircraft possible, because that is just what I want to talk about. I might say that by and large the area I am referring to would be quite satisfied with one good air service. We are not yet at the stage where we are worrying about two or more.
The minister may recall that earlier this year I exchanged some correspondence with him with respect to the establishment of an aeroplane float at the settlement known as Whaletown on the coast of British Columbia. In the last letter I received from him concerning this subject some little time ago he said he was having a review made of the matter and expected to inform me about it later.
I am not rising on the subject of the Whale-town aeroplane float at this moment primarily because I want the minister to give me an answer concerning this particular float on the floor of the house today,* but I am rising at this time because I do feel the provision of aeroplane floats appears at the moment to be in somewhat of an administrative no-man's-land. I asked some questions earlier

this year concerning how many installations of this kind the department has on the British Columbia coast, and I believe I could count the number on less than the fingers of one hand.
I think the minister will realize that a great deal of our air travel on the coast is carried on by planes which land and take off from the water; and because I feel this is a matter of importance I wanted to bring it to his attention under the discussion of the administration of air services.
Accompanying some of the correspondence that originated from the people at Whale-town in respect to this float was a diagram which I think illustrates very well the point I am trying to make. They submitted a sketch of some existing floats which were put in by the Department of Public Works in that area, and their suggestion was that by the simple addition of an extra float which would not be held in place by the ordinary piling arrangements but by anchor cables so there would be no obstructions to the landing of planes at the float, smaller planes could land there. I think the illustration makes clear a situation which I feel the minister should consider.
As I understand it, this is a matter which comes under the air services division but as far as I am concerned from what looking into the matter I have done I quite frankly have been led to wonder if this is not a matter which could not be looked after more effectively and expeditously by the marine services division, because of the fact that generally speaking these floats up and down the coast are installations which were put in for the use of boats and vessels, and are the concern of the marine services division and the marine agent of the district.
If this matter were looked into I feel that because of the long and close consultation that has existed between the marine services division and the Department of Public Works, provision could be made for the installation of floats that would be suitable for aeroplane landings in many of the smaller centres without the necessity of providing special installations intended solely for the use of planes. I feel this is something that could materially increase the available places that are suitable for aeroplane service without in the long run adding any great additional cost to the facilities on the west coast.
I hope the minister will give consideration to an examination of the administrative setup with respect to these aeroplane floats. Within the next few years I can foresee that there are going to be a great many requests for additional floats which can serve as floating airports for the smaller planes that
Supply-Transport
fly our coast. It seems to me that if this matter were studied at this time it might be possible to evolve a plan of providing such facilities at a good deal less cost than would be involved if all such requests for this type of installation were channelled directly through the air services division and involved special votes or allocations for that purpose.
In many cases, as far as I can see, all that would be required would be to work out a plan with the Department of Public Works to ensure that when some of the floats are installed the present arrangements, whereby they are held in place with piles which project above the deck level of the floats and constitute a hazard to planes, would be changed in order to remove the possibility of wing damage. Because of the hazard of the projection it is impossible for planes to use many of the existing installations except during very calm weather. I hope the minister will give me some indication as to whether he would be prepared to look into the various aspects of the matter that I have put before him.

I have in my hand a copy of a letter which was sent to the minister. Since he has been busy with these estimates, it is possible he has not yet read it. It comes from the president of the electrical, radio and machine workers' union at Hamilton and inquires from him with reference to the granting of a contract for the radar sets which will constitute the cross-country civilian radar network. It quotes a press report of a month or so ago in which it was stated that these radar sets are being produced to the specifications of the Department of Transport by a company in Waltham, Massachusetts.
The specific questions which are asked in this letter are whether or not any company in Canada was given an opportunity to undertake this work in the first place. In the event that it was thought by the department that Canadian companies were not yet equipped to do it, I would doubt that, because certain Canadian companies have gone into this work extensively in latter years. They ask whether or not any encouragement had been given them to go into this field.
I wonder whether the minister would answer these questions. Was an opportunity given to any Canadian company to undertake construction of these sets?

I think I can deal with this matter very quickly. I received a letter from the union this morning, and I have already dispatched a reply to it. I should like to say to the hon. member that this is substantially the information I conveyed to the union.

Supply-Transport
When it came to ordering these 15 surveillance radar units public tenders were called, and the lowest tender was that of Raytheon Manufacturing Company of Waltham. As they were public tenders, everybody had an opportunity of bidding, and some of the Canadian companies did bid.
Do you remember how many?

I think there were four or five companies altogether that tendered. I am sorry to say it, but the Canadian prices were much higher than those of Raytheon; in fact the nearest bid was $1,400,000 higher than that of Raytheon.
What proportion of the total price would that be?

It is probably approximately 20 to 25 per cent, or perhaps even over 25 per cent. My recollection of the exact figure is not very clear, but the point I want to emphasize is that not only was Raytheon the lowest tenderer but it agreed with a firm in Kitchener, Ontario, to establish a Canadian subsidiary for the carrying out of this work. That decision and the fact that it was awarded the contract meant that through the subsidiary it was possible for other Canadian manufacturers to develop a very large part of this order by subcontract. So really not only do the Canadian taxpayers save well over a million dollars as the result of our accepting a lower tender, but a new industry is going to be established and there will be subcontracting work in Canada.

I recognize that the minister's reply to my question is plausible, but I pointed out that some of these Canadian companies have been working for many years, and at great expense, in the development of this field, and some of them have produced amazing results. I am not sure, when it boils right down to what is best in the long run for the Canadian taxpayer, that so much of a net saving actually results to the taxpayer. There are such things as corporation profits, and so on, which would enter into it, and it would take more time and research than I have been able to put on this matter.
The minister said he received his letter this morning; I did not receive my copy until this afternoon. I have not been able to go into it, but it seems to me that when a contract is awarded to a United States company there are a great many ramifications to the awarding of that contract other than the fact that it is going to cost 20 per cent less.
It may be that some of those are covered by the taxation that will accrue to federal

coffers from the subsidiary company in particular, provided that company is taxed as a Canadian corporation. There may be a difference there, but if there is to be a difference in the amount of tax paid, then it seems to me that this matter of a 20 or 25 per cent spread in the price should be considered in the light also of the taxation which the respective companies will pay to the government of Canada through the Minister of National Revenue.
Item agreed to.

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude Richardson (St. Lawrence-St. George) moved
subtopic: SIGNATURE LOAN AND FINANCE COMPANY
speechtext: the third reading of Bill No. 166, to incorporate Signature Loan and Finance Company.

subtopic: SIGNATURE LOAN AND FINANCE COMPANY
speechtext:
It is the
intention of this group to oppose third reading of this bill. We are conscious of the fact that this is the last opportunity on which it may be presented at this session. Since the bill was passed in the committee-if my memory serves me right there were only four votes against it-on this occasion my hon. friends in the Conservative party joined my hon. friends on the government side to set up this incorporation; and since the majority was large we think that we should not use any device to hold up the legislation. But we believe we should have an opportunity to stand up and be counted in regard to our opposition to it, because we do not wish to be associated with those who vote for this incorporation.
We have the peculiar situation here of a group insisting upon incorporation under this bill after the representative of the company time after time declared in the committee that the action of the government under Bill No. 51, which puts some limit on the amount of interest which may be charged by such companies, threatened to put them completely out of business. We find that the promoters of this bill are persisting in their original intention to go ahead with the incorporation and, according to the statement of their colleagues, go broke in the process. However, we were never convinced in any case that they would be going broke in the process.
Branches of these small loans companies are spreading out all over this country. In our opinion the amount of credit of this particular type has become too great. It might be argued, and with some reason, that perhaps competition helps; that if you have one more company join the throng it may

have some effect in the bringing down of interest rates. At the hearings the president of the Canadian small loans association made an answer to a question I put to him which was rather surprising to me, but he knows his business. He said that in his opinion the amount of interest charged would make no difference to the amount of business done. That seems almost incredible but I suppose what it means is that people who are in the condition where they have to borrow money from these institutions are so desperate for money that the rate of interest is not even considered, or not mathematically worked out.
We are not too hopeful, then, that the addition of another company to the number already existing will have the effect competitive-wise of bringing down the interest rate to the borrower. One more company will mean something else. It will certainly mean more advertising. It will mean more branch offices being opened in the cities of this country. It will mean more bright neon lights and more places into which unfortunate people may be lured in the hope of improving their financial position by adding to the amount of their debt.
It is admitted that there is some need for this type of service, but as I suggested in committee at another stage of the bill we are already well supplied with facilities which, if they were only generally known, could carry on in a better way anything that the small loans companies are doing for this type of borrower. I shall now refer to what I mean, because I think it is reasonable that I should be able to bring forward alternatives. We certainly think that the banks could play a more active part in this business. The Canadian Bank of Commerce has already shown its ability in the field, and while the rate of interest is somewhat higher than in the case of the credit unions because they have the habit of discounting the loan before they make it, nevertheless the chairman of the Canadian Bank of Commerce said that they were making a profit at a rate of interest of between 10 and 11 per cent. We would urge upon the other chartered banks of Canada that they have some social responsibility so far as this matter is concerned.
As another alternative we suggest that the bill should not be passed because the facilities of the credit unions and the caisses populates in the province of Quebec are already being used to perform a function which this company would duplicate in the matter of the lending of money, and are giving a service which cannot be duplicated by these small loans companies. We had evidence in the
Private Bills
committee that kindred companies to the company we are now asked to incorporate are allowed by law to charge 26.8 per cent per annum. I use the term "per annum" advisedly. In referring to the matter I think such a term should be used because it is generally understood by most people who have anything to do with these companies, while it is rather difficult to figure out what a rate of 1 per cent or 2 per cent per month means.
I would suggest that from the evidence we had these alternatives, notably the credit unions, should be given serious consideration; because in comparing the rates which this company, if incorporated, will charge with the rates of the credit unions we find there is a tremendous difference. Evidence was given to the committee that under the present set-up a loan of $500 could cost the borrower $100 more over the two-year course of the loan when borrowed from one of these finance companies compared with the same amount of money borrowed from the Caisses Populaires Desjardins.
In my own province the average rate charged by the credit union is for a start 1 per cent per month, but as many of my friends from the west know, and I presume the same is true of the east, the credit unions have been notable for their tremendous growth in co-operation and we quite often have a rate of one-half of 1 per cent per month. Then we have the added feature of their excellent method of insuring loans, so that in the case of the death of the borrower those who inherit the estate of the deceased will not be harassed in the matter of paying the debt. So great is the benefit from that sort of thing that many people whom I know have joined one of these credit unions-

Private Bills
You have had the example of some other ministers doing the same sort of thing and we know with what result.
I had been saying that there were alternatives to this type of company and I had been giving the reasons why I think they should be used. I am relating strictly what happened in the committee when this particular bill was under discussion; and may I say that the very people who wanted to set up this corporation decried the credit unions because you have to be a member of a credit union. Everybody knows that where two or three are gathered together, if I may use that phrase, and want to set up an organization of this kind they can do it without the least trouble on a geographical, occupational or any other suitable basis. Rather than having a company of this sort simply interested in lending money, getting dividends from that money and paying them to their shareholders, we are interested in the type of thing which promotes thrift in the first place and which serves the purposes which this small loans company will serve if it is set up.
That is why I would rather see people use facilities which encourage thrift, which accommodate them temporarily and provide them with a guaranteed system of insurance. Let me say to the minister quite frankly that I am interested in the success of the credit union movement, which after all is simply the principle of co-operation applied to the small loans field. For the reasons I have advanced we do not want to endorse the opinion of those members of the committee who voted for the setting up of this company, and on that account we propose to call a vote upon this particular measure.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
474. Air services administration, $816,760.

When the work of the committee was interrupted at five o'clock I had just risen to make some comments on item 474. I find it rather difficult

to deal with the three things I want to mention because of the overlapping of the minister's department with that of trade and commerce as it applies to Trans-Canada Air Lines. The minister's department deals with the airports, so I feel I should deal with the airport at London first and then just refer to T.C.A.
The minister will recall that about a year and a half ago the hon. member for Middlesex West, the hon. member for London and myself along with his worship the mayor of the city of London and some of his council, as well as representatives of the chamber of commerce presented the views of the city of London as they relate to the airport there. At that time the plea was not for the beginning of new runways but the completion of them. There is one full length runway now being used by the Department of National Defence, and there is another runway which it is proposed should be extended so that jet planes and the Viscounts now in use on T.C.A. could use that airport. At the time this delegation waited on the minister I should say, in all fairness to the minister, that he promised nothing and he has kept his promise.
The city of London is quite concerned about this, because it appears as if the Department of Transport regards London as a whistle stop in their Trans-Canada plans. It would appear as if the Department of National Defence regards the city in the same light because of the grounding of No. 420 squadron. It has been adequately pointed out that there is a lack of air transport for an airborne army, yet we have a well established airport in a thickly populated area, which is not being used to advantage. It is a very vital area, also, when you consider Windsor, London, Sarnia, Woodstock, Brantford and Hamilton are all within close proximity of that London airport, yet they are given the go-by.
Some time ago it was reported that there would be 13 major airport radar installations across Canada, and that one of those 13 installations was to be made at London, Ontario. Now for some unexplained reason it is mooted that London is going to be given a smaller installation. The reason given was that there would be overlapping between London and Toronto. Be that as it may, there is a lot of overlapping in other government departments and it does not seem to worry them a great deal. It would not cost a great deal to extend the one other runway so it could service the Viscounts that are now in use, so I am asking the minister to give that very serious consideration for the immediate future.
There was a transport department official before a Senate committee, and he said
Supply-Transport
London would get a full scale weather station. This has been requested by the city of London and the surrounding area because of the importance of weather reports not only to T.C.A. and the air activities in the vicinity, but because of their importance to farmers who are so dependent on the weather. I hope the minister, when he replies, will say that this weather station is going to be installed in the very near future.
I mentioned earlier that the Department of Transport, the Department of Trade and Commerce and national defence are all tied up in this airport business at London. I should think, in view of the fact the Minister of Trade and Commerce has gas lines, air lines and party lines in his hands, he would transfer Trans-Canada Air Lines to the Minister of Transport.

I am sure I am flattered by the suggestion that I should have more work to do, but it is not one to which I shall accede very readily.
I would like to reply very briefly to what the hon. member has just said about the airport at London. My recollection is that it was not a year and a half ago that this delegation called on me, but something like six months ago. It may, of course, be the length of the session that has made the time seem longer, but my impression is it was in the early part of this year that I received the delegation and, of course, I have received representations from the hon. member and also from the hon. member for Middlesex West.
I should tell members of the committee that I believe the extension of the second runway at London has a high priority. We have been giving consideration to the matter, and I know that Trans-Canada would like to establish Viscount service on a permanent basis. The difficulty is, of course-there is the difficulty of money; there is never enough to do all the projects-there is really the basic difficulty of getting the technical personnel that we need to carry out all those projects. Hon. members all know that when you develop capable individuals and engineers, they are a very fair target for private enterprise which can and does offer them much higher salaries than the government can afford to pay.
My great apprehension with regard to these future projects is that of the difficulty of finding the skilled personnel we need for the work, and being able to carry out the projects in the highly active situation in which we are living at the present time. I would tell my hon. friend that we are fully conscious of the needs of London, and he does not need to

Supply-Transport
feel for an instant that it is being forgotten or that it is being relegated to an inferior position.

I have only one question I should like to ask the minister. Vancouver is growing very rapidly; international plane travel is growing very rapidly. I know that the airport in Vancouver is still owned on the local level. Have there been any further changes in negotiation or plans as between the ownership on the local level and on the federal level? This is the important question. In view of the growth of plane travel and the growth of Vancouver, what are the plans of the federal government, either on their own or in co-operation with Vancouver, for the expansion and enlargement of that airport so the Vancouver airport can take its rightful place as a major airfield of this country?

Mr. Chairman, when I went to the west coast last October I had the privilege and pleasure of meeting the mayor of Vancouver and some of the members of the airport commission. We discussed the present situation, and we were all in agreement that the question which merited the most immediate attention was that of providing additional terminal facilities. It was quite clear that had the responsibility for doing so been discharged by the city of Vancouver the legal formalities would have taken a very long time to accomplish, and since we realized this we said at once we were ready to make arrangements with the city of Vancouver by which we would finance the expansion of the existing terminal building, and an agreement was reached in principle at that time as to the expansion of that building.
I perhaps might add that since our discussion then they have had the plans and specifications for the work prepared. They have called for tenders. Unfortunately it appears that the cost is going to be greater than we estimated, but we have told them that we were agreeable to the increase in cost, and I think the conclusion of the action or document or agreement between the department and the city is a matter of a few weeks' time. At all events, we agreed that the expansion of the terminal building should be proceeded with first, as quickly as possible, and I think no stone has been left unturned to make that a reality.
So far as the airport as a whole is concerned, the hon. member knows that a substantial part of the area used for the airport belongs to the city of Vancouver. At an earlier date arrangements had been considered by which the department would

acquire the rights of the city for a consideration, I believe in the neighbourhood of $1 million. The proposal was submitted to a referendum and, as I think the hon. member will probably recall, the referendum was defeated and the city therefore has remained the owner of the airport. In the meanwhile, I cannot help thinking that so far as aviation is concerned, the question of whether the city owns the airport or whether the department owns it does not change materially the usefulness of the airport, and therefore the question of the title is secondary to the question of the terminal building.
I informed the mayor and the airport commission that we would be perfectly willing to re-examine the question of the department taking over the international airport, and suggested to them that they should submit to us a statement of the capital expenditures which were made by the city since the offer of $1 million was made some years ago. I say without any criticism whatsoever that this information has not yet been submitted to us by the city authorities.

I have another question on the same subject. I agree with the minister the question of the ownership is very definitely of a secondary nature. What I had in mind when I asked the question was this. About 18 months ago all the members of parliament of the lower mainland area were called to a meeting of the commission and a number of members of the council. The position was explained, to the effect that in a period of about 10 years a great many millions of dollars would have to be spent at the airport to complete almost a new plant. What I wanted to find out from the minister was whether any definite acceptance by his department had taken place on this 10-year period of the development of the airport?

I would just like to say to the hon. gentleman that really the question of whether the city owns the airport or whether the department owns it is not material to the carrying out of the program of capital improvements that would require to be made.
I am quite unable to give the hon. gentleman information as to what the program contemplated, but I do assure him that the question of who owns the airport or who operates it is not material to the program itself. It is our feeling, because we consider it to be a federal responsibility, that if the extension of a runway is required, or if the provision of an additional runway is required, or other facilities, that is something we should do, and that is one of the principal reasons why personally I do not attach vital importance to the question of title to the airport. I can

merely repeat that if Vancouver is anxious that we should take it over we are perfectly ready to discuss the matter with them at any time.
1 wish to ask the minister one question. He did not deal with whether a full-scale weather station was contemplated for London. What are the plans?

Well, Mr. Chairman, my
deputy minister tells me that we have no plans for the establishment at London of further meteorological facilities. In that field in particular it is exceedingly difficult for us to recruit trained personnel, and I do not think the additional facilities which the hon. gentleman contemplated are really needed at this particular time. At all events, we are not in a position to deal with it at the moment.
Mr. Chairman, according to my information one of the minister's officials, in giving evidence before a senate committee, said this was in the books.
Yes, I heard the hon. gentleman say that; but I must admit it came somewhat as a surprise to me.

May I say a brief word on this matter. I was very glad to hear the minister say that London airport is not being forgotten and that something is going to be done about it because, like my colleague for Middlesex East, it affects me very much and a great many other hon. members in this house from that area. Hon. members are probably aware that London airport serves not only London but the very rich industrial area of western Ontario, Stratford, St. Thomas, Woodstock, and Sarnia, and the rich agricultural area around.
There is one other matter that I should like to mention in about a minute's time, and it is this. It is quite apparent that there is no competitive business with respect to the Trans-Canada Air Lines run between Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto, London and Windsor. Since no competition is in the air, so to speak, at the moment I certainly hope the minister will recommend to T.C.A. that something be done to increase the service on that run. A person who uses that service finds it is almost impossible to obtain a reservation no matter how far in advance he makes application, and it is particularly difficult to obtain reservations on week ends.
Hon. members know it is sometimes necessary to visit one's constituency and return as quickly as possible. It has been my experience and that of many others that you cannot get reservations on that particular run.
Supply-Transport
If no competition is envisaged let us at least have more aircraft. I know the minister tells us it is difficult to get technical people and money, of course, is alleged to be a consideration in this case, but I do wish something would be done about it. I know a great many people who would like to fly by T.C.A. between London, Toronto, Ottawa, Montreal and Windsor, and the only reason they do not do so is because they cannot obtain reservations. If there is not going to be competition let us have more planes.
There is just one more thing I would like to add in this respect. T.C.A. cannot be very anxious to obtain business for this particular branch of the air line. As I understand it, formerly there were certain inducements offered to travel by T.C.A. No doubt this was done in the early stages to accustom people to the idea of flying. I was informed that commercial travellers used to get special rates on T.C.A. I am also told that other transportation companies such as the C.P.R. used to get some slight commission for selling T.C.A. tickets, but that is no longer the case. In addition to that I understand they cannot even telephone to make reservations for London or Toronto, wherever it may be.
It seems to me that if what I have said is true, and I am informed that these are the facts, T.C.A. cannot be looking for business. Particularly in view of the great difficulty one encounters in obtaining accommodation on this particular T.C.A. run I certainly think the minister and his department, if they are not considering competition, should at least consider increasing the number of flights between the points I have mentioned.

Mr. Chairman, before we leave this item I wish to express to the minister the gratitude of the Lethbridge constituency for the improvement which is being made in the airport there. Word has reached me that the tenders are in, the lowest tender has been accepted and all they are waiting for now is for the minister to let them know whether they are to finish the airport with asphalt or with cement.

Item agreed to.

Mr. Chairman, I have just a word to say concerning this item, which involves radio aids to air and marine navigation. This matter is becoming of more importance daily to the small transport companies. I would like to point out to the minister that there is increasing difficulty in getting wave lengths allotted to these small companies. From the standpoint of

Supp ly-Transport
safety it is becoming increasingly important that wave lengths be made available to the smaller types of operations.
It seems to me that the minister should reassess the requirements of the industry in this respect in order to see if we can squeeze out a few more wave bands for their use.
