Mr. Chairman, there is one question I would like to ask the minister on this item. Would the minister tell the committee what role the Department of Transport plays in the construction and operation of the mid-Canada line?

Mr. Chairman, my information is that the only expenditure which is included in the estimates of the Department of Transport for the mid-Canada line relates to items in the marine services-that is, transportation by sea-with which we have already dealt. We have no others.
What I had in mind was the role of the Department of Transport "in the construction and operation of the mid-Canada line.
My deputy minister tells me the answer to the question is that we have no role whatever in the matter except so far as the allocating of wave lengths is concerned.
You have no role whatever in the construction?
No.

When the line is in operation will the Department of Transport have any responsibility? We have been told during the discussion of other estimates that the Bell Telephone Company would be operating it, but I understood that the Department of Transport was involved some way or other. That may be wrong, but perhaps the minister could inform me.

I would like to say, Mr. Chairman, we do not expect to have any responsibilities in connection with the mid-Canada line when it becomes operative. Our present responsibilities are two-fold, as I

said a minute ago, and involve first the allotment of wave lengths and second a small part that we play in the ship to shore movement, both of which come under marine services which have already been discussed.
What is the situation with regard to the distant early warning line?

Item agreed to.
Radio Act and regulations-
478.	Administration, operation and maintenance, including contributions as Canada's share of the administrative costs of various international radio, telegraph and telephone conferences, as detailed in the estimates, $1,691,165.

Mr. Chairman, I made a few remarks concerning the general subject of the Radio Act when I spoke on March 16, and I did so at that time in the hope that when we reached the estimates of this department the minister might be prepared to make some comment on the questions I raised. I realize that was quite a while ago and I do not know whether or not the minister took any notes at the time. If he has I will not take any of the time of the committee to restate any of the points I raised.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman spoke about the increasing congestion of radio frequencies available for the use of fishermen, particularly in British Columbia, known as the fishermen's band 2318. He said the fishermen would welcome a greater measure of control over the use of that band. I will tell him that we are trying to accomplish this, but I am sure he will appreciate the difficulty of our task.
There is also the question of fishermen who operate small vessels objecting to the fact that some of the larger vessels employ high powered sets, and those who employ low powered sets in the area find themselves obliterated from the air. We hope by the process of education to persuade them to use better equipment, and we think that better sets will produce better results.

I had one other question with regard to the licensing of operators and the possibility that some of the fishermen who are affected will have to make long journeys to take examinations. Has there been any formulation of policy with respect to the question of licensing operators?

According to my note, it is a question of staff. If we had more staff it would not be necessary for us to ask these

people to go to Vancouver or Victoria in order to write these examinations as operators of radio stations. If and when we have more staff, I hope we can make a change in that situation.

The minister has again made reference to the question of staff. When he spoke on March 16 he also made a reference to this matter in respect of the question of radio interference, and inspection to avoid it. I think the house should give sympathetic consideration to the plight of the minister in respect of this matter of the insufficient staff, because in doing so we are giving sympathetic consideration to the problems that affect many of us as citizens.
I would suggest that the other members of the government should take note of what the minister has said and see whether we cannot do something about this matter. I had made some notes earlier about bringing up the matter of interference from the ordinary radio stations. I do not want to make an extended speech on the matter now, but I know it is a continuing problem in my area. If, as the minister suggests, the crux of the problem is the insufficiency of staff and, I presume, insufficiency of funds to pay and train them, I am happy to see the Minister of Finance has just come into the house and I hope he will do something to assist his colleague to meet this problem.

Item agreed to.
Telegraph and telephone service-
480. Administration, operation and maintenance, $515,320.

I should like to make a formal protest to the minister on the closing of the telegraph line north of Meadow Lake on July 1. I hope another look can be taken at this proposition, because it has been there for a number of years. It was put there by a Liberal government, not as a money-making proposition-if that had been the consideration I do not think it would have been put there in the first place-but to provide communication and a certain humanitarian service in an area that is sparsely settled. At least it was sparsely settled at that time, but it is not nearly as sparsely settled now.
This is the particular area of northern Saskatchewan where the people are also denied the family allowance, and between these two things I think they are wondering whether they are not being taken particular advantage of as compared with other people in the province. This line has served a great need over a number of years. It is used by the R.C.M.P. in the area, and naturally on my last trip through there both the R.C.M.P.
Supply-Transport
officers and the assistant agents of the Indian branch protested vehemently to me that the removal of this service was going to impede them in their work. I think representations have been made to that effect to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration by his Indian agents.
The hospitals in the area are small and scattered. There is only one doctor within 150 miles, and on many occasions major operations have been performed by the sisters at places like Portage la Loche on instructions from the doctor over this telegraph line. They have performed amputations and many such things. I should hope the minister would have a further look at this before it is discontinued. As I have said, it was put in there by a Liberal government on humanitarian grounds, for which I hope we are noted, and I hope this will still be regarded one of the guiding principles of the party.

Item agreed to.
Meteorological division-
483. Administration, operation and maintenance, $8,164,815.

In the Globe and Mail of March 13 this year there was an article headed "Weather Office Taxed to Limit, Official Claims". It said:
The resources of Canadian weather forecasting are taxed to the limit by the demands of aviation, the controller of dominion meteorological service said last night.
In an address to the board of trade club in the King Edward hotel, Andrew Thomson said "we really are pressed beyond what we can do."
We just want to ask the minister whether the allocation of funds here is going to put the department in a position to handle the requirements facing it, especially air traffic requirements.
I would merely say that the difficulty is not one of funds. It is that of getting trained personnel.
Is an attempt being made by the department to get personnel, because this would appear to be rather serious?
We are doing our best to get additional staff.

Item agreed to.
Civil aviation division-
485. Control of civil aviation, including the administration of the Aeronautics Act and regulations issued thereunder, $1,102,846.

Would the
minister reply to the suggestion I made that in future cases of accident investigations, where there is an indication that responsibility might lie on the operating party, he

Supply-Transport
might consider that the composition of the board of inquiry might include, say, a representative of the R.C.A.F., a representative of his department and a representative from outside?

In two or three cases that I can think of the inquiries have been presided over by a member of the judiciary. We have had outside members on the board of inquiry. I do not think I can lay down any rule of universal application. I can assure the hon. member, though, that we are anxious that these inquiries should be as complete as possible, even if perhaps they may lead to a conclusion that somebody in the department has not done all that he should have done. Again it is the difficulty of getting the right people at the right time. I would not wish to subscribe to the idea that the position should be always the same and that we should always have a judge. We have to have a certain amount of discretion, and in a general way we have appointed competent people to undertake these investigations.

Item agreed to.
Airways and airports-*
Operation and maintenance-
4S6. Civil aviation services, $9,855,840.

On this item, I should like to place one problem before the minister. As he knows, several attempts have been made to get a secondary airport in the vicinity of Vancouver for the use of light aircraft. Different sites have been mentioned. As I understand it, as yet no definite decision has been made by the government. Last year I brought up this question by way of urging upon the minister that he should not under any consideration agree to the establishment of a secondary airport at Spanish Banks, and the minister said at that time that he had not completed his investigations but that he was inclined to agree with me that it would be very unwise to take this property for a secondary airport. I thought that had been settled.
The hon. member is right.
If the minister can assure the committee now that under no circumstances will Spanish Banks be taken for a secondary airport, then that is all I want to know.

I should like to reassure the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra that no serious consideration is being given to the establishment of a secondary airport at Spanish Banks. To say "never" would be too categorical, but I will say that we are not considering it at this time. We are considering the possibility of a secondary airport at

White Rock and we are also considering what use can be made of Langley Prairie, but Spanish Banks is not being given serious consideration.

Can the minister assure us that no move to place an airport there will be taken without ample warning being given? The city council has gone on record against it, the parks board is against it and the university is against it. It is adjacent to a residential district, and the residents are all against it. It would be the worst kind of tragedy to take that beach, which is probably the most frequented in the whole of the Vancouver area, for an airport. What was the minister going to say?

I was going to try to answer the hon. gentleman. I was going to say quite frankly that personally I have been very much impressed by the arguments that have been advanced against the use of Spanish Banks for a secondary airport, and it would take a great change in my approach to the problem to say that it was going to receive serious consideration.

Would the minister look into the possibility of having the old Jericho air base, which is adjacent to this beach, turned over to the city for use as a park and as part of the beach? That air base was really established for seaplanes shortly after the first war, I think. It is used very little for flying. As a matter of fact, I know that a year or two ago it was used as an armoury for one of the anti-aircraft units. I do not suppose it comes under the minister's department. I think it is under the Department of National Defence.
It is, and I suggest that perhaps when the Minister of National Defence next has his estimates before the house the hon. member try twisting his arm instead of mine.

The Minister of National
Defence lives in my riding and very near this air base. Perhaps the Minister of Transport will help me to work on him in order to see that this air base is turned over as a park.

Mr. Chairman, I want to ask one question and I am not certain whether it comes under 486 or 488. The details of 486 would indicate that it comes under that item, but the amount of the money spent would indicate that it might come under 488. It may not come under either, but I will ask my question and the minister can answer.
There seems to be some misunderstanding among employees who are civil servants as to the rates of pay that are paid at one site or location compared with the rates of pay at

73S9
another location for the same type of work. This matter has been drawn to my attention and I have tried to explain that there must be an explanation. However, it leads to dissatisfaction among employees if they hear that at a neighbouring airport an employee doing the same kind of work is receiving more pay.

So far as classified positions are concerned, they are the same regardless of the airport involved. However, for labour engaged at prevailing rates the prevailing rate at one airport may be lower or higher than at another. Obviously when we are considering prevailing rate labour we are considering something that is essentially local. We cannot pay less than the prevailing rate in the neighbourhood, nor do I think that we should pay more.

These observations will apply to the next three items. This is the last item of the air estimates. In closing the discussion on these items I should just like to say that I was very much interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Meadow Lake. He gave a factual account of

Supply-Transport
the situation in the far north. In some respects he did not see eye to eye with me in the observations which I have made, but I think his remarks confirm what I have said previously, namely that the strangling of competition at the top has had its effect right down through the industry. As a start I think we might do one thing. speechtext:
It being after six o'clock I do leave the chair.
It being fifteen minutes after six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
As an introduction to some of the remarks I intend to make, I may say that I do not know whether the minister has any idea of the kind of country from which I come.
If the hon. gentleman would not take too long, I might be able to get up there this year.

I shall not be very long. We live in perhaps one of the best farming communities there is anywhere. We have some of the best farms and some of the best farmers you will find anywhere in Canada. For a long time we have been trying to entice industries to come up to our smaller towns. We have been having some success.
Now, however, the Canadian National wants to eliminate some of our train service. I would suggest to the minister that instead of eliminating some of the train service they should give us a little more service. Then they would have no reason to want to discontinue the trains in that section of the country. For example, not so long ago the railway installed a new scale at Palmerston to weigh the rock that comes down from the Durham pit. It is a small scale and they cannot weigh a car. They have to weigh half a car at a time. Can you imagine any outfit trying to make money on a road, pulling a car in and weighing one half and then weighing the other half. Not long ago 42 cars of stone came down at one time, and they were all night weighing the 42 cars. Then they were only guessing. They might just as well have weighed one car and guessed at the rest. This will give you an idea of the kind of service we are getting.
Last Saturday night, August 4, two old passenger cars left Toronto, old cars with oil lamps and some of the lamps were not working. There was no drinking water for the passengers. You would actually think the railway was trying to see how bad they could make the service so nobody would use the trains. I am not going to give names, but the railway put a foreman on that section not long ago, a young man of good education but with no experience. He was trying to tell some of these old trainmen who have been on there for 40 years what to do. This is another example of what they are doing in that section of the country.
The other day the post office was instructed to find some other means of transportation after September 30, because the train service would be discontinued. We went to the transport commission's offices and we could not find any evidence there that they were going to discontinue these trains. We went to the Post Office Department and they told us they had been informed the service would be discontinued after September 30. Naturally they had to find some other way of carrying the mail, so they undertook to call for tenders for trucks to deliver the mail. This was not because they wanted to do that, but they were forced to do it. We want an opportunity to appear before the board of transport commissioners to state our case.

We believe these trains are not losing money but are making money. If we got improved service they would pay well.
Would the hon. gentleman tell me to which trains he is referring?

Those trains out of Palmerston north and west on the Kincardine line and the Southampton line. Apparently they are going to cut off the service on both those lines. I believe there is another section of the line which goes up to Goderich about which I saw an item in the newspaper to the effect that service is going to be discontinued. This is a good section of the country and there are good farms up there.
I should like to refer to a statement made last night by the hon. member for Wellington South. I was not in the house at the time, but according to Hansard of August 9, 1956, page 7342, this is what he said:
I spoke on this item four years ago along with the hon. member for Bruce, the hon. member for Perth and the hon. member for Wellington North. We approached the minister on this same issue and after our representations and private presentations these lines were not closed up. I think it should appear on the record that members from this district four years ago prevented this line from being closed.
I was here at that time, and I would hate to be so narrow-minded as to make a statement like that. I am getting sick and tired of hon. members getting up in this house and stating that unless you belong to the government side you are of no benefit here. This is not the only time that has happened. It has happened frequently in this house, and it is not very becoming to those who make these utterances. As a matter of fact I am glad to be able to state that the departments have a much wider vision than this particular gentleman has, because I have gone to them on different occasions and was very well treated. I have not any complaints to make, but I do not think that kind of thing should be left unchallenged.
I have not very much more to say. I wrote the president of the railroad and told him what we wanted to do. I wanted to find out who was putting the pressure on to have this service discontinued. Of course I have not had time to have a reply yet. All we want is a chance to go before the board of transport commissioners and state our case. I do not think we will have any difficulty in keeping the service.

employees of the Montreal and Southern Counties Railway. There is one section in the statutes of 1955, volume 1, chapter 29, which gives the Canadian National Railways the opportunity of operating buses. At the same time I wish to say that the Victoria bridge is now in very good condition for such a bus transport service, and I wish to thank the minister in that behalf, because I know he had some influence with the Canadian National Railways to get this thing going. The bus service between Montreal

and the south shore should cause no trouble whatsoever. Therefore i hope the best possible company will be chosen. If we cannot get the best company, I hope the Canadian National Railways will operate it.

I wish to voice a protest against the action of the Canadian National Railways in attempting to close so many of the agencies in my constituency. I say "attempting" because fortunately the board of transport commissioners has refused them permission to close a number of them. Would the minister not agree that at any point where there is a certain volume of business and where the volume of business is at least as great as, or greater than, it has been in the past, the C.N.R. should attempt to maintain the agencies and leave the agents there? For instance, the minister must be familiar with the town of Munson, in one of the best wheat-growing districts in Alberta and a heavy producer of grain. They sought the right to close that agency last year. Then again, they sought the right to close the one in Huxley, in another very prosperous mixed farming district. Fortunately, in both these cases the board of transport commissioners refused to grant the permission.
I think the C.N.R. are acting out of all reason in apparently making an attempt to close out the agencies at so many points. It should not be merely a question of revenue. Surely the question of service should be taken into consideration. I hope the minister will try to use his influence with the railway to see that this policy of closing down agencies is halted. An effort should be made to keep them from attempting to close more of these agencies. I do not know how many have been closed in my constituency in the past five years, but it is a considerable number.

Mr. Chairman, last week I quoted the decision of the board of transport commissioners with respect to the Canadian National Railways, and tonight I wish to make some reference to commuter rates, particularly to the decision handed down by the board on an application of the Canadian passenger association for a rescission of the board's order, 75234, dated September, 1950, which ruled that the railways were entitled to out of pocket costs and authorized as an adjustment in the Toronto area a 100 per cent increase in the commuter fares, to be effective in three stages, the first being 50 per cent on September 30, 1954; the second 25 per cent on March 31, 1955; and the third, 25 per cent on September 30, 1955, making the full 100 per cent within a year and a half. The railways stated that this would only give them a fighting chance to break

even, and asked that the board give them discretionary power to fix commuter rates at a higher level if the new rates proved to be below the compensatory level. The municipalities contested this and contended that 35 per cent would be sufficient.
The board further held that the railways had on their own initiative over the years set their own rates in given areas, and that their allowance of a 50 per cent increase in all areas other than in the Toronto area was an interim judgment while further evidence was gathered, and their investigation would have to be continued before they could give a final judgment.
I might mention that the Canadian National Railways said that 44 per cent of their passenger traffic was commuters. This increase which was granted to the railways augmented their revenue considerably. The increase granted to the railways on commuter fares should have supplied sufficient incentive for them to make an improvement in service on the commuter lines, but that did not turn out to be the case. In fact they did not follow that up. In the submission of the president of the Canadian National Railways to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects on January 19, 1956, Mr. Gordon made a statement to this effect. He said that the commuter service is an unprofitable operation because the benefits of the service are localized at present in Halifax, Saint John, Quebec, Montreal and Toronto; and with the future expansion, plus the past expansion, there would be additional demands for new or more service to new centres. The demand would be made by municipalities finding that they would have to have extra service.
The conclusion was that the railway commuter service was unprofitable at any level of fares that the commuters could afford to pay. No matter what rate was set it would not be satisfactory. Naturally you would expect that. He said that the decentralization of urban communities, to what he termed metropolitan satellite residential districts, meant that they must have high-cost streets and arterial systems for motor vehicles and road transportation, and that this created a demand for increasing railway commuter service. That is natural, too. He said, "Under these circumstances, if a municipality will make good our losses we are prepared to design a commuter service adequate to the demand" and he offered this suggestion, which is a proposition, as the only practical solution for the future.
Then later on, when he appeared before the railways and shipping committee, he was questioned about this submission to the royal commission. He said that what he had said

before the royal commission had been distorted. He said he had not asked for subsidies from the municipalities, but he did state that commuter service was unprofitable, and if any municipality wanted to talk to the railways about expanding commuter service they must talk in terms of benefit to their communities, that the whole of Canada should not have to pay for the losses on the Canadian National Railways to benefit one area only. He said that if more commuter service is to be built, then there should be a contribution from the area that receives the benefit. Then he made the further observation that all solutions so far advanced had missed the cardinal point that the railway facilities around Toronto were at complete saturation now and it is a problem to handle present business and traffic. It was mentioned that they had come to the end of the possibility of supplying better service.
Another statement which appeared in the press was made by Mr. Kyle, vice president of the central region of the Canadian National Railways. He had this to say in a well thought-out statement. It is physically not possible. The Canadian National Railways should not superimpose fast regular service on existing lines already jammed with long-haul freight and passenger trains. He said that local industries were coming into the metro areas so fast that his lines are likely to be overcrowded for years ahead. He said the Toronto union station cannot handle the present traffic, let alone thousands of additional commuters.
Then after making that statement he had this to offer. One solution is to parallel present lines and build a new station, and he proffered an estimate on the cost of purchasing and building a right of way of over $100 million, which the municipality would have to pay. I think it is time we had a clear understanding concerning how and why the railways received their charters and franchises. Was it not for the prime purpose of moving goods and people, and on the understanding that the extent of their prosperity and progress would hinge on the kind of service they gave as is the case in any other enterprise?
When the country was sparsely populated the railways were given aid to get started and were further assisted in lean years; but they were also required to strive for top service in the carriage of goods and passengers and were expected to apply all their effort to increase every phase of their operations and provide for the continual expansion of their systems. Have the railways ever tried to find out what kind of service the commuters required and what rate they
Supply-Transport
could pay or would be prepared to pay in any given area? Have they ever given a fast, improved service with reasonable frequency and punctuality as an inducement to increase patronage? Obviously the answer is that they have not. Instead they have curtailed the number of runs, as we heard here tonight, and have complained about the handicaps they encountered. Other enterprises encounter difficulties but they manage to overcome them, and the railways have not done this. They have always adopted a defeatist attitude.
One can see by their statements that they would prefer to haul only the freight traffic because it is the most profitable.
Turn another page.

If the railways do not co-operate in providing service that will take commuters to their work where they fabricate the merchandise that the railways will haul, where will the railways get their freight traffic?
Let us see what the railways have done by way of planning in the past for inevitable future expansion. They have done nothing to secure property and needed facilities, and on their own admission they are stymied concerning the Toronto area because they failed to take such provident steps. They have not kept pace with progress in the last three decades and now they say to the municipalities, and this applies particularly to metropolitan Toronto, "You must pay cash on the barrelhead for the kind of service you want, to provide us with the physical assets which we failed to acquire during the past 30 years." How brazen can they get? Well, the last proposition of the Canadian National Railways is a glaring example.
Over 30 years ago Sir Adam Beck had envisaged a great network of electrically operated radial railways in a gradual expansion plan for Ontario that would have provided a fast commuter service as well as an intercity service. He advanced his campaign to the point of public acceptance, and then a whole horde of those who were envious of the success of the hydro project, wrathfully joined forces with those who personally disliked him because of his aggressive nature and adamant stand and opposed his radial project, and they were successful in their campaign which effectively scuttled the radial plan.
Where does the Canadian National Railways enter into this picture? What has it done concerning commuter rates and services? Through different days and different ways people forget over the years. Sir Henry Thornton, then president of the Canadian National Railways, aligned himself with

Supply-Transport
those who stood in opposition to Sir Adam Beck; and the weight of Sir Henry Thornton's prestige gave the necessary impetus to the campaign and he is given the credit for having scuttled Sir Adam Beck's radial plan. Even at this date the Canadian National Railways cannot detach itself from the culpability of Sir Henry Thornton's actions.
Sir Adam Beck died shortly afterwards. Had he lived to see his radial plan put in operation there would be no commuter problem in Ontario today. Is it any wonder that there should be resentment at the Canadian National Railways' cash on the barrelhead proposition, when they had not done anything to provide an efficient commuter service? They have made no attempt during the three decades I have referred to.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few words to say under the item concerning the board of transport commissioners. This is the board which hears applications from the railway companies for permission to increase freight rates and alter passenger service and depot facilities and various other things having to do with the railways. I might say that I have always been appreciative of the service they have rendered and the attention they have paid to any recommendations or briefs which have been presented on behalf of groups or communities when the railways have made such applications. In the past year out of four applications which have been made for the closing of stations or depots in my constituency, in only one case was the application granted and the company given permission to withdraw its depot service.
There is an application before the board of transport commissioners at this time which is of great importance to all producers in western Canada. That is the application of the railway companies for permission to charge demurrage on cars which are still loaded with grain at terminal elevators 48 hours after reaching that point.

Mr. Chairman, I raised a point of order last Saturday when an hon. member was attempting to discuss the question of demurrage, and I think the Chair ruled that inasmuch as this case was now before the board of transport commissioners and was therefore sub judice it was not in conformity with parliamentary practice to discuss the issue of such a case.

I realize, Mr. Chairman, that the application has been heard and there has merely been a postponement to September 10 which will of course completely remove the possibility of our discussing it in this house if the Chair so rules.
[Mr. Small.!
Speaking aside from the board itself, I would point out to the minister that there is a great need for storage space at terminal elevators, and also that the railway companies have a great need for cars for the movement of grain. I hope the problem can be solved in order that for the movement of grain cars will be made available which have been tied up at critical times in the past, which has caused the producers to suffer. It is also my hope that something can be done to prevent the cost of this increase being passed on to the already overburdened producers. I shall leave this subject at this point if that is the ruling of the minister-
It certainly is not my ruling.

I am sorry; the ruling of the chairman with reference to the minister. I would now like to ask a question. In cases such as I have mentioned does the board carry out the policy of the government or are they left entirely to reach a judgment based on their own findings?

Mr. Chairman, I can say immediately they are a quasi-judicial body. The government does not attempt to direct the board as to the course of action they should take in any circumstances. Hearings are conducted before the board and evidence is adduced by all parties interested in the particular case. The board then renders its decision. In some cases there is an appeal to the supreme court and in some cases there is an appeal to the governor in council, so there really is no reason why the governor in council should intervene. I can assure the hon. member that the government does not attempt to influence the board in any way whatsoever.
I would like to refer to the position of the transport controller.
That item has already passed.
What item does that come under?
Under the first item.
Under administration?
Yes.
The whole matter is discussed under the one item?
Yes.

That is really not covered by the item, but I can dispose of it by saying that when the hon. gentleman raised the question I drew the matter forthwith to the attention of the transport controller. I think the hon. gentleman should not really expect me to act as a sort of messenger between the members representing different constituencies and the transport controller. If that were added to my already numerous duties I fear that my other work would be sadly neglected.
I was not asking the minister to do that. He requested that I should call any particular incident to his attention, and I merely did so.
I think I shall have to withdraw that offer.

The minister indicated a little while ago that the question I wish to raise should be asked on this item. It is in regard to the Northern Alberta Railways having been under construction for a great number of years. I do not think there are any physical reasons why it should be still under construction; very likely it is a device for maintaining a little higher freight rate. This railway is now far removed from a trappers' railway and is carrying a tremendous amount of freight, and I do not doubt that that is now a fairly remunerative part of the railway's operations. This deals with the Canadian maritime commission. Inasmuch as questions were raised earlier in the discussion with regard to the government's interest in Canada's merchant marine, I should like to take this occasion to make public some changes that have been made in connection with both the replacement plan and the transfer plan. I think the quickest way for me to deal with the matter is to read the short statement I have in this connection.
Supply-Transport
Immediately after the war the government sold the bulk of its war-built fleet to private Canadian operators, subject to a flag covenant requiring that the ships be kept on Canadian registry. To overcome some of the practical difficulties arising from this covenant the government, on the recommendation of the Canadian maritime commission adopted two measures:	the replacement plan and the
transfer plan.
The replacement plan enables the owner, with the approval of the Minister of Transport, to sell his ship off Canadian registry, free of the flag covenant, provided the proceeds of sale are deposited in escrow to be used for the acquisition of an acceptable replacement for the ship sold. Up to the present time in all cases where escrow funds have been used, the replacement vessel became subject to the flag covenant without any limit of time.
The transfer plan enables the owner to transfer his ship from Canadian to United Kingdom registry under special arrangements. This allows him to overcome the handicap of the substantially higher costs of operating on Canadian registry and to carry cargoes for sterling freights, of which the profit is convertible into Canadian dollars.
To encourage a greater use of the replacement plan, the government has now approved certain modifications of the flag covenant on ships acquired in whole or in part with escrow funds. These modifications were recommended by the maritime commission after extensive discussions with the Canadian shipowners' association. They do not apply, however, to the original flag covenant which was assumed by the purchasers of ships from the crown and which remains unchanged.
From now on the flag covenant for a replacement vessel will be for five years if the vessel is built in Canada for the operator effecting such replacement, and for ten years in all other cases. This modified flag covenant will be applicable to the replacements which have already been effected.
As a further encouragement to the shipowner to replace the vessel originally sold by the crown and to invest his own funds for this purpose, the terms of the replacement plan have been modified so that if during the currency of the flag covenant the owner sells his replacement vessel off Canadian registry, he will be obliged to redeposit in escrow only a proportionate part of the escrow funds used for its acquisition. This proportionate part will be the sum which represents the same proportion of the

Supply-Transport
escrow funds invested in the vessel as the unexpired term of the flag covenant bears to the full term of the flag covenant. For example, if a vessel subject to a five-year flag covenant were sold when three years of the term remained to run, then three-fifths of the amount of the escrow funds invested will require to be redeposited in escrow.
Holders of escrow funds will now be allowed to use them for tanker type ships.
Furthermore, the use of escrow funds will be allowed for improvements to a vessel, excluding of course ordinary repairs and maintenance, whether effected in Canada or abroad, subject to conditions generally similar to those applying to the acquisition of a replacement vessel, unless modified by the maritime commission in special circumstances. The commission envisages that there would be no extension of the flag covenant if the conversion or alteration were carried out at the time of the purchase of the vessel. If, on the other hand, the conversion were carried out later, but during the life of the flag covenant, the commission does envisage an extension of the covenant based upon the amount of money used, expressed as a percentage of the original cost to the owner of the vessel. For such expenditures of up to 10 per cent of the cost of the vessel, there would be no extension of the flag covenant, but thereafter, in the case of a Canadian-built vessel with a five-year flag covenant, for each 20 per cent or part thereof one additional year would be added to the covenant, and in the case of a vessel built outside of Canada with a ten-year flag covenant, for each 10 per cent or part thereof one additional year would be added to the covenant.
Further modifications will also be brought about in the realm of capital cost allowances. At present, for income tax purposes, it is compulsory to pool vessels that have an exemption from recapture of depreciation, under section 4 of the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act, with other vessels that do not benefit from this exemption. Consequently, when the owner disposes of some or all of the vessels so pooled, his exemption can readily become dependent upon the order in which they are sold. Broadly speaking, if the qualified ships are sold earlier and the unqualified ships later, the sale of the qualified ships may serve to wipe out the undepreciated value of the class. This situation could be remedied by permitting an owner, if he so elects, to treat as a separate prescribed class any vessel or vessels that qualify under section 4 of the act; that is, a vessel the proceeds of sale

of which had been used for replacement under conditions satisfactory to the commission.
It is the government's intention to recommend to parliament at the next session the legislation required to remedy this situation.
At present under the income tax regulations a ship does not qualify for any capital allowances until she is, and I quote, "a ship as defined in the Canada Shipping Act". In practice this has meant that a ship must be practically completely built before being eligible for depreciation unless she is built under the provisions of the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act. Generally speaking, therefore, the shipowner was placed in a position inferior to that of other enterprises which can claim capital cost allowances on assets as progress payments are made during construction. It is the government's intention to take the necessary steps to remedy this situation.
I must apologize, Mr. Chairman, for the length of the statement, particularly at this stage of the discussion, but I am sure hon. members will realize that these are significant changes in the provisions of the transfer plan and the replacement plan, and I think they go a long way toward meeting the requests which Canadian shipowners have made in recent months. Broadly speaking, while this does not represent all that we have been asked to do, it represents a very high proportion of what we have been asked to do and I think it is a very constructive move.

Mr. Chairman, it would be quite impossible to deal with the minister's announcement this evening because we have not had an opportunity to study the details of the statement. However, as I understood him, it is in effect a change in the transfer and replacement plans and the purpose is to make it easier for shipowners to get modern ships. That would apply almost entirely to ships owned by Canadian shipping companies which are now flying the British flag and are manned entirely by British officers and seamen. It seems to be of no help whatever in re-establishing a Canadian merchant marine. In fact it may make it even more difficult to establish such a marine under the Canadian flag, because it is easing the covenant which provides that the shipowners must keep their ships under the Canadian flag if they wish to get certain benefits.
It is for the replacements that the covenant is being eased.

That certainly will not make it more likely that we will have a larger Canadian merchant marine. I believe the time is long past when the government should have

adopted a policy to bring about the establishment of a modern Canadian merchant navy. But here again in the announcement tonight of this new policy the government is evading that question, failing to meet the main question, which is whether or not the Canadian flag is to fly on the high seas and Canadians are to have the opportunity of manning ships of their own country.
It is very appropriate that this discussion should come up under a vote for the Canadian maritime commission. As the minister knows, that commission was set up after the second world war, and for very definite purposes. It was given a very high status. I have here the act entitled the Canadian Maritime Commission Act, which was passed in 1947. Section 4 of the act provides that the commission and the persons employed by the commission shall constitute a department of government over which the minister shall preside, and the chairman of the commission was given the status of a deputy minister.
In other words this was not just an ordinary commission. This commission was set up as one of the most important commissions under the whole governmental framework. It was also given very wide powers. They are contained in section 6, which reads as follows:
The commission shall consider and recommend to the minister from time to time such policies and measures as it considers necessary-
For the following purposes, which I should like to emphasize in my remarks.
-for the operation, maintenance, manning and development of a merchant marine and a shipbuilding and ship repairing industry commensurate with Canadian maritime needs.
Then the act went on to outline in some detail the different ways in which these powers were to be exercised. Some of us had been advocating the setting up of a Canadian maritime commission for some years before the government actually took that step. When the bill was introduced in 1947 it was introduced by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce. I have here Hansard for June 23, 1947, and should like to quote from page 4514 what that minister had to say with regard to the functions of this commission. He said:
The bill seeks to set up an authoritative body to advise the government on shipping and shipbuilding matters and to administer certain matters relating to those industries. The proposed commission is to consist of three full-time officials who, as a body corporate-
This is important when we consider what has happened since.
-will be responsible to and subject to the direction of the Minister of Transport.
Then he went on further:
The function of the commission in its advisory capacity is to consider and recommend to the
Supply-Transport
minister such policies and measures as it considers necessary for the operation, maintenance, manning and development of a merchant marine and a shipbuilding and ship repairing industry, commensurate with our maritime needs.
The minister also dealt with the power given to the commission to set up advisory committees from the various industries which were interested in the merchant navy. He said:
It is our thought, amongst others, that a standing advisory committee consisting of representatives of ship operators, shipbuilders, and seafaring personnel should be set up as soon as possible, which will provide a forum for discussion on a number of matters concerning the efficiency and development of the industries.
Before I go on to point out how the government has failed to keep the commission functioning as it was meant to function in the first place, I should just like to read what this same minister said about the need for Canada to have a merchant navy, as found at page 4214 of Hansard of June 16, 1947. He said:
I would not suggest that we have a merchant navy sufficient to carry all our exports. I would suggest that we require a merchant navy able to carry a substantial part of our exports and to protect Canada's position in the matter of freight rates and other problems of carriage. Today-
That was in 1947.
-we are the fourth maritime nation in the world-
We have slipped a long, long way since then.
-and when the boats now on British register are returned we shall probably be the third maritime nation in the world. Whether Canada in the future will require to maintain that position is a question for the maritime commission to study, so that it will be in a position to advise the government. Being a shipping and shipbuilding nation at the moment, it is important that we shall remain a shipping and shipbuilding nation.
I propose to point out now the tragedy of what has happened in spite of that statement made in 1947 by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce. A commission was duly set up. The chairman chosen was Mr. J. V. Clyne of Vancouver, a marine law expert and a man who understood thoroughly the problems of shipping. I think the minister will agree with that statement.
He did a magnificent job here as chairman of the Canadian maritime commission. The first three reports were submitted by Mr. Clyne. Then he resigned, and shortly afterwards was appointed to the supreme court of British Columbia, where he is rendering the same type of efficient service that he rendered here. Under Mr. Clyne the advisory committees were set up. The second report contained an analysis of the whole history of

Supp ly-Transport
Canada's shipping, shipbuilding and ship repairing industries and contained clear recommendations. I believe those advisory committees have never met since Mr. Clyne resigned.
When it came to replacing him, who was chosen? The man chosen was the deputy minister of the Department of Transport, who had probably as many duties as or more duties than any other deputy minister here in Ottawa. By that very action the government made it impossible for this Canadian maritime commission to function as it was intended to function, and the decline has continued steadily. I am not criticizing the present chairman, although I believe he has other duties to perform in addition to his duties as chairman of this commission.
The second member is one of the key men in the St. Lawrence seaway authority. He succeeded Mr. Lessard as the deputy minister of the Department of Transport, and is still a member of this commission. You can realize at once how much time he would have to work on those problems which were allotted to this commission under the original statute. The third member, Mr. Angus McGugan, unfortunately passed away a few weeks ago. He too had done excellent work, and I should like to pay tribute to his memory. That is the position of this maritime commission today.
My first suggestion to the minister is that he take steps at once to reconstitute this commission as it was intended to be in the first place. It was never intended to be just a back-office branch of the Department of Transport. It was intended to be set up as an almost independent commission able to consult with the people interested from coast to coast and to make independent recommendations to the government.
The policy recommended by this commission is contained in the second report. I am not going into any details other than to say that they recommended that Canada should have 50 dry cargo vessels. The tonnage was to be 500,000. They were not to be old wartime ships. The objective was 50 modern dry cargo vessels. That was the recommendation in 1949. The previous year this commission had worked out a transfer plan under which a large number of Canada's wartime merchant vessels were transferred to United Kingdom registry, where they remain to this day.
That was done because at the time ship owners were unable to operate these ships profitably under the Canadian flag, but the result was that all the Canadian sailors on those ships were put on the beach. They lost their jobs. Ever since then these ships have

been under British registry, have been manned by British sailors and have been directed by the British government.
Within the last few days I believe that at least three of those ships have been requisitioned for service in connection with the trouble at Suez. That just shows how little they can can be regarded as Canadian ships. They are directly under the British authorities, and they are only Canadian in that they are owned by Canadian shipping companies which, of course, pay taxes to the Canadian government.
And, of course, they may be recalled at any time by the Canadian government.

It will be very interesting if the minister will table the exchange of notes or the agreement with regard to these ships that were transferred to United Kingdom registry. When they can be requisitioned and sent to the Suez, as has been done within the last week, it does not look as though the Canadian government has very much authority over them. Furthermore, they are not modern vessels. They are all old, slow wartime ships.
So much for the transfer plan which is being modified to some extent by the policy announced by the minister this evening. In 1949 the replacement plan was arranged. I am not sure whether it was in 1948 or 1949 that the plan was commenced.
I believe it was 1948.
I think that is right; I think it was $3J million.

Under that policy $34 million was set aside, which amount was to subsidize 35 or 40 vessels so they would be able to operate without loss. That plan was in operation only for the one year, but as a result of that assistance given in 1949, these ships were able to operate successfully until 1953. In 1953 there was trouble again. Ocean freights were down, the ships were having trouble, and another plan was announced on November 12, 1953. That plan- just as is the plan which the minister has announced tonight-was aimed primarily at easing the replacement plan, making it easier for the ship owners to get new ships. The

announcement with regard to that plan had this interesting final paragraph:
It is further announced that, after due consideration, the government has decided that the request made by the Canadian shipowners' association for operating subsidy could not be approved at the present time. However, if it appears feasible to establish modern Canadian flag vessels on certain routes that would be of a benefit to the development of Canadian trade, Mr. Chevrier indicated that consideration might be given at a later date as to whether or not some form of assistance ought to be provided in such cases.
In other words, that was a half promise that there would be a subsidy for the operation of Canadian vessels on certain routes which were the most vital to Canada. Nothing ever came of that last proposal. There never has been any such assistance given. From time to time changes have been made in the replacement plan, just as a change has been made this evening.
Last year we raised this question in the house, of the situation of the merchant navy, and the minister told us he was concerned about it and was going to study it after the house prorogued. Well, he studied it until November and then an announcement was made which, in effect, said that the government would do nothing.
Which, in effect, said the government was not going to subsidize these ships.

In effect it said the government was simply going to allow what did remain of the merchant navy to disappear. The government accepted absolutely no responsibility for the rebuilding of the Canadian deep sea fleet. This was in November and now, nine months later, we are getting this watered-down change in the transfer and replacement plan.
What is the situation of the Canadian deep sea fleet today? I have here the ninth report of the Canadian maritime commission, and it shows that of this fleet which ranked fourth in the world in 1947, we now have left under Canadian registry five 10,000 tonners; six 4,700 tonners; three diesel cargo ships and three other cargo ships, for a total of 17. All these 10,000 tonners and the 4,700 tonners are old wartime ships. There are three of the 10,000 tonners that belong to Dosco and are engaged in trade between Newfoundland and Sydney, Nova Scotia; one belongs to the Mersey Paper Company of Liverpool, Nova Scotia and the fifth, although it is under Canadian registry, is in Italy. It has not been back here for years and is manned by an Italian crew, with the exception of a British captain and a British chief engineer.
Then of the 4,700 tonners, incidentally reduced by one since last year, five belong
67509-470J
Supply-Transport
to the C.N.R. and one is owned by the Mersey Paper Company. The diesel cargo vessels, of which there are three, all belong to the C.N.R. The other three cargo vessels all belong to the Mersey Paper Company. The tonnage of Canada's deep sea fleet of cargo vessels is now down to 87,085 tons, the lowest it has been in 40 or 50 years.
In spite of what we did during the war in the way of building, manning and operating merchant vessels, only the crews are left to man these ships. All the rest of the Canadian merchant seamen are on the beach; have had to find other jobs. The ship-owning companies, which are experienced and have done a good job, are working toward liquidation. Perhaps this new plan will stave that off for a while, but that is the trend into which the shipping companies of Canada have been falling.
So far as the amount of our own trade that we carry is concerned, that is set out also in this report. It shows that in 1954, which is the latest year for which figures are given, Canadian vessels carried only 2-1 per cent of Canada's overseas trade, down from 1947 when it was 20-2 per cent. United Kingdom ships carried 33-8 per cent, down from 45-2 per cent in 1947. The ships of other flags in 1954 carried 64-1 per cent of Canada's trade, and in 1947 they only carried 34 -6 per cent. I venture to say that in 1955 the percentage carried in Canadian vessels was even lower than 2-1 per cent, and in 1956 it will be lower still.
In so far as shipbuilding is concerned, the only thing that has kept our shipyards active has been building for the Canadian navy. This report shows how that dropped off. Compared with 1954 there was a fall-off of 60 per cent in the gross tonnage and 50 per cent in the dollar value of ships delivered. Ship repairing is also dealt with. The total value of merchant and naval repair work completed in 1955 amounted to $27,039,805, and compared with 1954 this constituted a decrease of $11,104,723 or 29 per cent. This includes naval repair work. The average monthly employment in the industry, that is in the shipyards with 17 yards reporting, was 12,432, a decrease of nearly 20 per cent compared with 1954.
There is the sad story of what has been happening to Canada's deep sea fleet. At the same time, practically every other nation in the world has been building up its merchant navy. Switzerland, which does not touch the sea at all, has a much bigger merchant navy than Canada. We are building naval escort vessels costing millions of dollars. What are they going to escort? There are no Canadian merchant vessels for them to escort.

Supply-Transport
By the way, I should have given the figures for the Canadian-built ships which are under British registry. At the time this report was completed there were 99, and that was four less than the year before. Four of those ships have gone oil the register. This minister and his predecessor have said that we have these old ships under British registry and if trouble comes we can use them. Apparently there are two pools if war should come, the United Kingdom pool and the United States pool. These Canadian-built ships go into the United Kingdom pool, and Canada will have to fall back on the United States to supply any merchant vessels she might require.
The situation on our coasts is tragic. Of course, coming from the west coast I am particularly concerned about it, as are the east coast members about their coast. Here is a dispatch that appeared in one of the Vancouver newspapers on February 18 of this year. It is headed, "Canadian Registered Freighters Fading Fast". It reads:
Last year only six Canadian-registered deep sea vessels cleared the port of Vancouver. I think it is the lowest total of Canadian ships to sail from this port in the last 50 years. Ten years ago there were nearly 50 deep sea ships owned and registered in this port, carrying our lumber, wheat and other products all over the world. Most of those ships were built here. All of them carried Vancouver crews. Wherever one went in the world, those ships carried the name of the port of Vancouver.
Today there is not a single Vancouver-registered ship on the high seas.
Then there is this significant paragraph:
Rightly or wrongly, Ottawa has given up the ghost. The merchant service no longer exists, and all the royal commissions in the world won't bring it back to life against the hard facts of international competition.
I suggest that the minister go down and spend a weekend in a resort on the St. Lawrence river where he can watch the ships going up and down that river which is to constitute Canada's great inland seaway. I did that a few weeks ago. There is not one Canadian ocean-going ship operating on that seaway at the moment, and there is not going to be one unless the government changes its policy. Ships from Holland, Sweden, Norway, France, the United Kingdom and Germany are going up and down through that canal system even before the seaway is built, but not a sign of a Canadian vessel anywhere.
The eighth report of the commission set that out. It said:
There were 11 steamship lines operating regular ocean services to and from the great lakes in 1954. Including liners and tramps, 99 ships, none of which was under Canadian or United States registry, made 275 trips from overseas ports to the great lakes.
IMr. Green.]
In the ninth report we find the same situation; no Canadian ships, no United States ships, and a larger number of ships from the continent where they are building ships for the St. Lawrence trade.
