The United States has moved to meet this situation. In February the United States maritime administration stated that its trade from the great lakes to Europe would be considered essential, and under the terms of their law it became eligible for subsidy. I have a dispatch dated Washington, February 8, which says:
The United States maritime administration today made American ship operators on the great lakes eligible for government subsidies by declaring the ocean route between American lake ports and western Europe to be "essential" to U.S. trade and economy.
The aim, officials said at a press conference, is to permit the United States vessels to compete with cheaper foreign shipping.
The report goes on:
A reporter asked whether the subsidy would mean more competition for Canadian shipping.
"It will certainly be competitive," maritime administrator Clarence G. Morse replied. "We'll needle our operators to do their damndest."
He suggested the Canadian lake ports of Toronto, Hamilton, Windsor and Sarnia, Ontario, would benefit from increased trade.
I have other dispatches here, including the report of a speech made by our own minister, pointing out just exactly what that United States policy would do, and I do suggest to him that Canada should adopt a policy which would have the effect of putting a Canadian fleet on the St. Lawrence seaway to carry some of the Canadian goods overseas to Europe. Last year the minister criticized me by saying that I had not made any suggestions-
I was thinking the same thing this year.

The minister is thinking the same thing tonight. Well, I am a little bolder tonight. I do urge in all earnestness that the government delay no longer in adopting

a policy which will put a Canadian flag deep sea fleet in being again. It may mean subsidization. No subsidy would be required at the present time because the ocean rates are so high. In many of those intervening years Canadian ships could have earned their way had they been given some encouragement by the government, but even if there has to be subsidization in order to keep a minimum number of Canadian ships at sea, then let us face that necessity and subsidize them. I believe that at the present time subsidies certainly would not be as much as $100,000 a year; probably $75,000 a year would be sufficient.
Per ship.

Per ship, to keep those ships competing because the United Kingdom wages have gone up and, as I said, the freight rates are high. I do not believe it would cost this country very much money if a bold policy were adopted. Then I suggest that the government, having adopted the plan of having a merchant fleet, should appeal to the national spirit of the Canadian people. They are a maritime people. That has been shown time and again and, as a matter of fact, in the last war I believe the young men from the prairies made an outstanding record as Canadian sailors. Therefore it is not only a matter of the people on the coasts and on the St. Lawrence. Canada is now in a position where she could have a modern merchant navy, and it is far more important to us now than it has ever been, particularly because of the development of the St. Lawrence seaway.
I do urge upon the minister that he should not be content with this policy he announced tonight as the great cure-all. This is only a palliative. I do urge upon him that he see to it that his fellow ministers approve a policy which will once again put the Canadian flag on the high seas.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be very brief in replying to the hon. gentleman. He has adopted a very convenient line of argument. He has started with the recommendations which were made by the Canadian maritime commission in its first or second report, and he has very conveniently disregarded all that has happened since 1947; the fact that since 1947 other important shipping nations of the world have added materially to their shipping; the fact that the shipping market has changed entirely; the changes that have taken place in freight rates, and now the change that has taken place even with regard to these very vessels which constituted the nucleus of the Canadian merchant marine. He described the position
Supply-Transport
of the owners as working toward liquidation. Now, Mr. Chairman, the fact-
I said there was a trend toward liquidation.

Call it a trend toward liquidation, or working toward liquidation. I do not see very much difference between the two. The fact of the matter is that the owners of those vessels, which are now 99 in number, on the United Kingdom register bought those ships for an average price of around $400,000, and they can sell them today for prices varying from $700,000 to $1 million, notwithstanding the fact that they have been able to take depreciation on them during the intervening years.
The great difficulty in this matter is the tremendous disparity in operating costs on Canadian register in contrast with those on United Kingdom register. A moment ago the hon. gentleman seemed to imply that no subsidy was now required. Those are the words I thought he used; but the fact of the matter is that it is estimated that under present conditions it costs somewhere between $80,000 and $100,000 a year more to operate a 10,000 ton dry cargo vessel on Canadian register than it would to operate it on United Kingdom register. That is the crux of the situation.
When we discussed this matter last year and I told the hon. gentleman and other members of the committee that we were giving consideration to this problem of a Canadian merchant marine, that was an accurate statement of the facts. Consideration was given to the possibility of granting an annual subsidy to a limited number of modern vessels, but after the most careful consideration the government reached the conclusion that it would not be desirable to establish a system of annual subsidies to bonus operators of ships on Canadian register.
Following that announcement made last October I have had a number of interviews with representatives of the shipping owners, and I have suggested to them that we should consider the ways and means that should be taken in order to facilitate their operation of vessels even if it were necessary that they should operate them on United Kingdom register.
The conditions I have outlined tonight will, I think, do a great deal to stimulate the replacement of the present Park ships which are on United Kingdom register by new vessels which may be either on Canadian or United Kingdom register, depending on the circumstances; although, as I say, I think it is pretty clear that when Canadian costs are so much higher than those of the United

Supply-Transport
Kingdom there is a very natural tendency for an operator to desire to have his ship on United Kingdom register.
There is not really much doubt that they will be on United Kingdom register?

No, but sometimes taxation and other reasons militate against a simple solution, and consequently there may be cases in which an operator will keep his ship on Canadian register rather than transfer to United Kingdom register.
I want to make it clear to the committee that under the arrangements that have been concluded, the so-called transfer plan, these ships that have been transferred to United Kingdom register or retained on United Kingdom register, may be recalled by the Canadian government at any time.
I would much prefer it if conditions were such that ships operating with Canadian crews, and paying Canadian wages, and carrying out their repairs in Canadian yards, were able to compete in the international market for freight; but it is perfectly manifest that so long as our Canadian costs are so much higher than United Kingdom costs we cannot do so without introducing a policy of subsidy. I would like my hon. friend to tell me where we will stop if we start subsidizing h!s industry, because there are many other industries which would get along very nicely if the government would pay subsidies and thus enable them to meet the cost competition of other countries.
You are doing it every day in other cases.
I did not hear what the hon. gentleman said.

I would like to ask the minister what other industries want subsidies. I think almost every industry and everything else in Canada is subsidized and protected, and I do not see why we cannot do the same thing for our merchant fleet.

Mr. Chairman, when the hon. gentleman has an opportunity of carrying his opinions into effect it will be very interesting to see whether he will still preach the policy of subsidization.
I want to conclude by saying that one of the great difficulties we have been faced with up to now has been because the flag covenant originally contracted also applied to any new vessel that might be acquired or built as a replacement, ship operators, despite the most attractive price they could get for the ship they were operating, have hesitated to sell and have hesitated to effect replacements-because they were bound by the

same covenant to maintain the ship indefinitely on Canadian register. The situation under the modifications I referred to earlier is that if the ship is built in Canada the term of the covenant will be for five years, and if built elsewhere it will be for 10 years. In other words there is a definite limitation, and I believe a very real encouragement to replace and build in a Canadian yard.
What is gratifying, Mr. Chairman, is to find that the Canadian yards are receiving an increasing number of inquiries from people who desire to build in Canada. There again we are faced with similar difficulties. It costs approximately $1.60 to build in Canada something that you can build in the United Kingdom for $1.
But they can deliver much quicker.

Yes, they can deliver much quicker, as the hon. gentleman says, and for that reason Canadian shipyards are receiving inquiries in increasing numbers. I am hoping there will be more dry cargo vessels built this year than has been the case for a number of years past.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few brief remarks on this item. First of all I want to associate myself with the very fine review the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra has made of this extremely sad and outrageous situation that exists concerning our merchant fleet today. At the same time, Mr. Chairman, I want to be generous enough to say that I appreciate the difficulties the minister has in interesting his colleagues in the future of our fleet and our problems with respect to the sea.
There is no doubt about it, Mr. Chairman, our big difficulty is that we are a nation of landlubbers. That is one reason we have not a merchant fleet today. We are controlled inland by industrial central Canada. We do not have the background and the interest we should have in our coasts and their trade. Without carrying that thought further I want to say that probably the best example we can find in relation to our problem is the situation of the Canadian National Steamships West Indies fleet.
For quite a few years now we have let these ships operate from year to year without any definite future plans. We finally realized last year that they had a future, that there was some trade and some revenue there. The department has proceeded with a five-year plan now, and perhaps some credit is due to the minister. The fleet has been modernized, and we have taken that progressive step.
I say we should be making the same kind of plans for the future of our merchant fleet,

along the lines outlined by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, in order that Canada may take her place among the great trading nations of the world. The minister laid great stress on the fact that salaries and operating costs were a problem. Certainly they are a problem. We cannot blame our sailors who when they go to sea want the same conditions and salaries they enjoy at home, because we have a high standard of living in this country.
We do not blame them.
I am simply suggesting, Mr. Chairman, that our seamen want what they are accustomed to at home.
Of course they do.

We do not blame them for this but fortunately-or unfortunately, perhaps- we have a high standard of living in Canada. Some of us think it is slightly artificial, but we do have it. These men want the conditions to which they are accustomed, and when they are in competition with fleets from other parts of the world they have difficulty. The same difficulties exist in many of our industries in this country. How many of the industries in Canada today, apart from the few that are living off our natural resources, are not protected and subsidized to some extent? I make the plea that our merchant shipping fleet should have the same consideration. This is absolutely essential, and it accompanies the fact that we are emerging as a major power in this world.
One evening recently I mentioned the fact that 24 nations are meeting in London to discuss the Suez crisis, and Canada is not one of them. No responsibility; isn't that great? It may be very well to say we have no responsibility, but we know it is because we are not considered in the oceans of the world. How proud we would be to be able to see the Canadian red duster. We do not even have any argument about the flag that would be flown in all the parts of this world.
I say we have an example in the Canadian National Steamships where a little forward thinking might have helped the situation which, the department now admits, indicates a future with respect to trade in the Carrib-bean sea and related areas. I suggest that the salaries are an old excuse. It does not mean anything nowadays. We hold no brief for the seamen and their strikes in the past, but we have to wake up. We have to realize that central Canada is not everything in this country. We can talk of industry and the profits from war materials and some of the easy money we made in the last war, but we
Supply-Transport
still have to take our place at the council tables of the nations when war conditions are concerned.
Those are my serious thoughts, and in that connection I have a question to ask the minister. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra asked a question and the minister replied to it, but I do not think he went far enough. He asked what exactly are the terms of an agreement with respect to the return of these vessels from their registry in the United Kingdom. I think the minister said, "When they are needed." I should like to ask him whether he would give me a more specific answer.

The answer is very simple. The British government can at any time return those ships to Canadian registry if it so wishes; and any time the Canadian government desires that they be returned to Canadian registry they must be returned.
In other words, if we were to indicate at any time that we needed those ships back in Canadian waters, they would be our own without any strings attached?
Correct.

My second and final question is with regard to the inquiry I made of the minister concerning the brief of the naval officers' association of Canada, a very responsible body which convened in Montreal at an annual dominion association meeting about six weeks ago. There it was suggested that it was imperative that a merchant fleet be considered, and I think a subsidy was mentioned. At that time the minister said he would not comment but that he would look into their brief in detail.
Is he in a position now to say what he thinks of it? I admit that I have never seen the brief. The difficulty with any thought of promotion of the merchant fleet is that naval matters always receive first consideration; they are under a budget. But I feel personally that if a group of officers who know and understand the past history and record of the merchant navy say that we are in a serious state, then we should take cognizance of that. Would the minister comment on that?

What I have said in response to the comments of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra applies with equal force to such representations as have been made by the body to which the hon. gentleman has just referred. There cannot be two different answers to the same question.

May I ask the minister how it would be possible for Canada to man these ships if she did recall them from the

Supply-Transport
United Kingdom? I understand that the United Kingdom is now having great trouble in getting sufficient seamen to man her own ships. The Canadian seamen have all been shoved off on to the beach. How would Canada man these ships if she did recall them?

The problem of manning ships has arisen before. When these ships were built we needed men to operate them, and we got them. I think if an emergency arises and Canada decides to have these ships retransferred to Canadian registry, we would not do it in such a way that they would all arrive on the same day; we would do it in such a way that the manning facilities would be equal to the task.
What is the explanation for the United Kingdom government requisitioning these ships in the last week?
I take it that if these ships are on the registry of a particular country they are subject to the laws of the country of registry.
That is the whole point.
That is an advantage or disadvantage, depending on the circumstances. I cannot see that they are being exposed to any particular disadvantage in the circumstances.

Will the minister table the
agreements or the exchange of notes for whatever contains the agreement between Canada and the United Kingdom covering these ships.
I would have to look into that. I could not give an answer, either negatively or affirmatively, at this time.

May I follow that up by asking this. If the Canadian government indicated a need for the ships, would it be subject to the fact that the United Kingdom herself would not want them for any sort of emergency state?
What I said is perfectly clear, and the hon. gentleman has no reason to add those qualifications.

when it will be completed, and whether it will go into operation at the start of the tourist season next year?

I have a question that I have been asked to address to the minister by the hon. member for Verdun, who unfortunately had to leave. Would the minister be kind enough to tell the committee whether the site of the proposed bridge that is to span the St. Lawrence river at Nuns' island has been already chosen and, if so, would it be premature to disclose it now?

I believe the national harbours board has reached a decision as to the location of both ends of the bridge to cross the river by Nuns' island in Montreal, but I am unable to give an exact description of the site at either end. So far as the north end of the bridge is concerned, it has been the subject of discussions with the municipalities of the city of Montreal and the city of Verdun. So far as the south end is concerned, it has been the subject of conversations with representatives of the provincial government, but we have not received final approval from the provincial government of the site of the south end of the bridge.

Has
the minister made any progress in attempting to negotiate for a fire boat for Montreal harbour? I would point out to him that more and more, with the immediate advent

of the seaway, this is becoming a sheer necessity for that area. The St. Lawrence municipal bureau has made a study of it in conjunction with the shipping federation of Canada. They point out that if there were a fire in the channel in the area of Montreal harbour the seaway itself could very well be blocked for an indeterminate period of time.
I am not so much worried about that at this point, serious though it is, as the very simple fear that a day will -come, as it does in most harbours, when there is going to be a serious fire on board a vessel in the harbour. The fire fighting equipment in Montreal harbour consists of a few piddling little hoses on one or two tugs for which fire fighting is very definitely a secondary consideration, and when such a fire occurs the fire fighting equipment will be totally inadequate. People will die and the harbour will be disrupted.
The damage may be tremendous, and it will be almost completely because of a lack of liaison and a lack of activity on the part of the federal government in pushing this thing through. I realize the minister's argument is that it is partially the responsibility of the city of Montreal but I remind him again that the national harbours board is not the property of the city but the property of the federal government, and it is the federal government's prime responsibility to provide fire protection on the water side.
I would also point out to the house that the federal government is now putting up $33,000 a year for the city of Vancouver alone toward the operating costs of a fire boat, and it would seem to me that something like this should be done and done immediately in the city of Montreal.

May I say just a word on that subject. When I first became a member of the city council of Montreal in 1941 that subject was discussed. I think I may say it was one of those perennial subjects that were discussed on some occasion every year during the seven years I was a member of the municipal council. The hon. gentleman has just compared the situation in Vancouver with that in Montreal. The two harbours are not comparable. The fact is that the harbour of Montreal extends over a very considerable distance, and it is a fact that fire protection can be much better afforded by the very excellent fire department of the city of Montreal than if these facilities were to be provided by fire boats.
The speed in reaching the scene of a fire when the apparatus travels by road is so much greater than if it travels by water. In the past there have been fires on vessels in the harbour, and there were fires before 67509-471
Supply-Transport
I became a member of the city council. I think the fire department has dealt with them most capably and competently, and I do not really believe that an improvement -can be made on what they are doing.
The subject has not been recently discussed between the city authorities and the national harbours board, but if the city authorities feel that the subject should be re-examined we would be very happy to study any fresh representations they would like to make.

Is
the minister prepared to make a grant to the city of Montreal on the same basis as that to the city of Vancouver if the city should desire it?
As I said, the two harbours are not comparable, and I could not give a categorical answer, either yes or no, to the hon. gentleman's question.

Mr. Chairman, I have a supplementary question with respect to the Nuns' island bridge. There is a great deal of interest in the bridge in my constituency, and I should like to know if the minister can tell me at this time the approximate date of commencement of construction and the approximate date of completion.

I am sorry, but I cannot give either the date on which the work will start or the date on which it will be finished. I will tell the hon. gentleman that Dr. Pratley and the firm of Lalonde and Valois have been retained for the preparation of the plans, and they have been engaged on the project for some months now. I think the work is progressing in its present stage as rapidly as can be expected.

Mr. Chairman, since we have been dealing with bridges, more particularly the Jacques Cartier bridge, without repeating the arguments I used, I should like to ask the Minister of Transport once again to be so kind as to tell us whether or not he has considered the many suggestions which were made to him for the abolition of toll charges on the Jacques Cartier and Victoria bridges. I understand that these tolls are still in force.
I wonder if it would not be possible, after considering the points we have brought up, to grant this request in the nearest future possible.
At any rate, if they are maintained, I suggest again that toll charges be applied to vehicles only, and not to passengers of automobiles crossing the bridge. I believe that revenues have increased considerably; there

Supply-Transport
are no more deficits. Again may I say that, if it is impossible to abolish toll charges altogether, I think that they could at least be limited to vehicles.
Now, there is another matter I had raised and upon which I would like to speak very briefly. It concerns the site of the toll collection booths. I had suggested that they be located at the south end of Jacques Cartier bridge simply because that would give the citizens of Montreal free access, without having to pay tolls, to St. Helen island, which belongs to them. This will hardly be news to the minister, since he is perfectly aware of the situation, having been a member of the municipal council. I repeat this request out of regard for the citizens of Montreal. It is only fair that they should be allowed to go to the island without having to pay the toll to cross the bridge.
Now, during the debate on the address, I had asked whether it would not be possible, at least on the Montreal bridges if not throughout the province and this country, to make toll charges uniform? That is to say, why would it not be possible to use the same tickets on the bridges which belong to the government as such or to the harbours board?
To sum up I would like to ask the minister to take into consideration the suggestions that I have put forward to the effect that toll charges be levied on vehicles alone, and not on passengers, that the people from Montreal be allowed to go into the St. Helen island without having to pay anything and, finally, that toll charges be made uniform on these various bridges. This would be until such time as toll charges are abolished altogether.

Mr. Chairman, I will answer very briefly the questions just put to me by the hon. member for St. Mary. First, that of toll charges on bridges. T may say that a committee was formed in early 1955 to study this whole question.
Following the studies made by that committee, we came to the conclusion that, for the time being at least, it would be preferable to consider the creation of new facilities, even toll facilities, rather than the abolition of present toll charges, a course that would deprive the population of Montreal of the benefits resulting from the construction of a new bridge. It is as a consequence of the studies made by that committee on toll charges and as a result of the representations submitted by the delegates of the city of Montreal that the government came to the conclusion that the construction of a new bridge through Nuns' island would be justified.
Following these recommendations, we studied the possibility of undertaking the

construction of a bridge through Nuns' island. The national harbours board is at present considering a change in rates so as to exempt automobile passengers. I must give at least a word of encouragement to the hon. member by telling him that it is the national harbours board intention, when rebuilding the approaches at the south end of the bridge, -which will be made necessary by the construction of the seaway-to locate the toll collection booths at the south end of the bridge and thus to provide facilities so that traffic will be delayed as little as possible.
The hon. member has asked for the abolition of the toll charges; we shall give him half a loaf since the collection booths will be located at the south end of the bridge.
I must tell him that there have recently been talks between the authorities of the C.N.R. and the national harbours board with a view to standardizing the tolls on both bridges; I do not know whether the required order in council has been passed, but the matter will be settled shortly.
As far as the St. Helen island matter is concerned, we are investigating the possibility of admitting free traffic going to St. Helen island, but there are certain difficulties for, as soon as people could cross the bridge free of charge, there would be too much congestion. 534. Loan to the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation in accordance with the provisions of section 14 of the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation Act for additions and betterments to facilities, $4,506,725.

This subject, as the minister well knows, has had a great deal of discussion in committee and also in the house, and in view of some of the minister's comments in the committee and the house I cannot help but observe that while the minister may have referred on another occasion to another cable company, the Commercial Cable Company, as being subsidized in an indirect way to the tune of around $10 million a year on a proposed coaxial cable-
Not $10 million a year.

I thank the hon. member and the minister. It is $1,600,000 a year for ten years. In view of the fact that loans are being made to Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation at the rate of $4 million or $5 million a year, one cannot help but reach the conclusion that at least an indirect form of subsidy is taking place here. I know the minister is going to say that the loans have to be repaid. So they do; but when they are government loans to a crown corporation I do not imagine there is any hurry about repaying the money. I do not think there is very much likelihood of a fire sale or bankruptcy proceedings taking place.
The hon. gentleman should start relating his remarks to reality.

The minister speaks about reality. If Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation does not pay back the loan, or does not pay the interest one year, I should like to know what the government are going to do about it. Are they going to sell the assets of the company? My remarks relate to reality. If they cannot pay back the loan and cannot pay their interest I suppose they will get a larger loan next year. However, that is just a passing observation in view of the many remarks that have been made in the house and in committee on previous occasions, and I realize I should not refer to them.
Supply-Transport
However, suggestions have been made that probably in the very near future television programs from Europe and the United Kingdom may be available in this country. Of course, as most hon. members know, there are at present only two ways of transmitting television programs successfully, by microwave relay or by coaxial cable. I think it very unlikely that television programs from Europe will be sent over here by microwave relay. It is not very likely that towers will be built in the middle of the Atlantic. The only other way would be by coaxial cable.
Previously, of course, as I have already mentioned, we have had reference to a proposed coaxial cable that the Commercial Cable Corporation wishes to lay with certain outlets in this country. It is also my understanding that at the present time Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation has an interest in a cable that the Bell Telephone Company is building, and expects to have certain channels in that cable. What I am curious about is this. Has the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation been consulted by the Department of Transport as to the interest of C.O.T.C. in the telephone company's coaxial cable with respect to television programs coming from Europe to this country?
Then there is a second point in which I am interested. When, in the fairly near future, these programs are being sent to this country, will it be the policy of the government to confine the transmission of these programs via coaxial cable wholly to the lines of communication operated by C.O.T.C., or will some sort of competition be allowed, for example, by the Commercial Cable Corporation?

Before the minister replies I think it should be pointed out that last year some $5,470,000 odd was voted to the corporation and this year the amount is approximately $4,500,000. I am also informed there is an additional amount in the supplementary estimates. It would appear that this is going to become common practice. This communication system apparently is going to grow from year to year, and the taxpayers are going to be required to put up money from year to year to provide for that growth. If we were in a field, as was the case at one time in the creation of the C.B.C., where it was felt that the private stations were not providing the type of programs that the government felt were needed, then there might be some justification for a continual line of credit

being extended. But I am certainly directed to a few words in the report of this company which read as follows:
. . . we shall also introduce a multiplicity of new telegraph circuits in sufficient numbers to meet adequately the needs of Canadian users for some years to come.
Right here there is an indication that, it is the intention of this crown corporation to take over completely, if at all possible, this means of communication. Yet at the same time-

Mr. Chairman, surely it is not necessary to go all over again the same arguments and the same debate that we had on the Telegraphs Act. What we are concerned with here, Mr. Chairman, is whether or not the amount of $4,506,000 should be placed at the disposal of C.O.T.C. as a loan. I am sure the minister jumped to the bait much too quickly. I had only one more sentence to go and that would have ended the problem from our standpoint.
I surrender.

My concluding sentence is this. Surely there is no necessity for this type of expenditure and for the type of control that has been vested in the minister to ensure that this corporation should advance from year to year, when it has been indicated very clearly that there has been an alternative method which would have provided all the things which are referred to in a report of this kind without the advancing of one dollar by this government.

subtopic: ARTHRITIC AND RHEUMATIC DISEASES
ARTHRITIC AND RHEUMATIC DISEASES
speechtext:
1.	How many Canadians suffer from arthritis and rheumatic diseases?
2.	What is the estimated annual cost to Canada in working time loss, and otherwise, because of these rheumatic diseases?
3.	Does the federal government give grants for basic research into the cause and cure of rheumatic diseases?
4.	If so, (a) what is the amount of such grant
for the year 1956-57;	(b) what universities are
beneficiaries of such grants?
5.	What is the total amount of the federal health grant allotted to the Canadian arthritis and rheumatism society during the past seven years?
Answer by: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of
National Health and Welfare):
1.	It is estimated from Canada's sickness survey and previous surveys that 225,000 disabled Canadians are suffering from arthritis and rheumatism. Of this number, 155,000 are severely or totally disabled.
2.	From the survey it was found that in persons suffering from arthritis symptoms were present for more than half the year. In persons suffering from rheumatism symptoms were present for about one-quarter of the year. During much of this time the person would be able to carry out his usual activities, which in the case of older people might consist of little more than self care. From information available at the present time, it is estimated that during a year approximately nine million days are lost from usual activity through arthritis and rheumatism. Of this loss from usual activity, over one-third applies to persons of 65 years and over.
3.	Yes.
4(a). $91,261; (b) McGill University, University of Montreal, Queen's University, University of Toronto, University of Western Ontario, University of British Columbia.
5. $330,670.

subsubtopic: SCHOOLS IN EUROPE
speechtext:
1.	How many Canadian children are attending national defence schools in Europe in (a) elementary schools; (b) high schools?
2.	How many Canadian teachers employed by national defence in Europe are in (a) elementary schools; (b) high schools?
3.	What is the estimated cost per pupil per year, taking into account salaries, transportation, rental of buildings and other cost factors for (a) elementary schools; (b) high schools?
Answer by: Hon. R. O. Campney (Minister of
National Defence):
1.	(a) 3,708 in grades one to eight; (b) 221 in grades nine to 13.
2.	(a) and (b) There are 145 elementary school teachers and 28 high school teachers in national defence schools in Europe. They are not directly employed by the Department of National Defence, but rather by school boards in Canada which have contracted with the department for the loan of teachers for two-year periods. The teachers' salaries are paid by the school boards, to protect superannuation and other benefits, and the school boards are reimbursed by the department.
3.	(a) and (b) The average estimated cost per pupil per year for elementary and high school grades is $256.52. Since high schools and elementary schools are as yet integrated in the same buildings, even to the extent that there is some interchange of subject-teaching between the two, no figures are available from which to show separately the per capita costs for elementary and high school pupils. The figure of $256.52 comprises the cost factors for salaries, supplies, transportation, heating, and rental of schools; it does not include small per capita costs for lighting, gas, and maintenance, which are incorporated in an over-all figure for married quarters, schools, and recreational areas.
